adrs.status_raw: Accepted. #1251 and #1253. adrs.text:
# 151. A capability that acts on a subscription is not found past a wrapper

Date: 2026-10-24

## Status

Accepted. #1251 and #1253.

Amends [ADR 118](0118-a-subscription-model-capability-marker-replaces-object-in-the-of-lookups.md) and
[ADR 119](0119-subscription-model-capability-gains-instance-side-lookups.md), where both
say the blocking lookups walk a `SubscriptionModelWrapper` chain for every capability.

## Context

Since 0.33.0 the blocking `SubscriptionModelCapability.capability(type)` answers `this` when the model implements
`type`, and otherwise unwraps one `SubscriptionModelWrapper` and asks the wrapped model. The static `findIn` methods,
`RepositionableSubscriptions.findIn` among them, call it. So a lookup on a wrapper that doesn't implement a capability
answers the model beneath the wrapper, and the caller then acts on that model as if the wrapper weren't there.

For a capability that only reads, that is what the caller wants. `IntrospectableSubscriptions.subscriptionIds()`
asked of a `DurableSubscriptionModel` is answered correctly by the model it wraps. For a capability that acts on a
subscription it is wrong, because a wrapper that keeps state for a subscription never hears about the action:

* `RepositionableSubscriptions.findIn(competingConsumerModel)` answers the model the
  `CompetingConsumerSubscriptionModel` wraps. A resume at a position through it resumes the subscription while the
  competing consumer still has it recorded as paused and holds no lease for it (#1251).
* `RepositionableSubscriptions.findIn(durableModel)` answers the MongoDB model under the
  `DurableSubscriptionModel`. A resume at a position through it moves the subscription without storing a checkpoint,
  so a restart before the next event resumes from the older stored checkpoint (#1253).
* `capability(CheckpointAwareSubscriptionModel.class)` on the stack the Spring Boot starter builds, a
  `CompetingConsumerSubscriptionModel` over a `CatchupSubscriptionModel` over a `DurableSubscriptionModel`, answers the
  `DurableSubscriptionModel`. A `subscribe` through that answer goes around both the catch-up and the competing
  consumer.

The reactor stack has no `SubscriptionModelWrapper`, so its `capability(type)` never unwraps and none of this applies
to it.

## Decision

### 1. The blocking default unwraps a wrapper only for a capability that observes

`capability(type)` answers `this` when the model implements `type`, as before. Past that, it unwraps a
`SubscriptionModelWrapper` only when `type` is one of these:

* `IntrospectableSubscriptions`, `ReplayAwareSubscriptions` and `HistoryRetainingSubscriptions`, which answer
  questions about subscriptions.
* `QuietPositionReportingSubscriptions`, which adds and removes a listener that is told positions. Another listener
  changes no wrapper's state.
* `Pushable`, which takes events in at the bottom of the stack. They reach every wrapper's action on the way up as
  usual.
* `HistoryLossReportingSubscriptions`. Its listener can answer `TakeOver` and so act on a subscription, which makes it
  the exception to the rule. It stays unwrapped because it is the SPI a catch-up model uses to hear about lost history
  from the MongoDB model under a `DurableSubscriptionModel`, and the `DurableSubscriptionModel` keeps its own state
  through its own listener in the same list. Making it answer only for itself would mean every wrapper forwarding it,
  and would change how a catch-up model takes over a subscription.

Every other capability acts on a subscription and is answered only by a model that implements it:
`Subscribable`, `CancellableSubscriptions` and every type built on it (`SubscriptionModelLifeCycle`,
`SubscriptionModel`, `CheckpointAwareSubscriptionModel`, `StreamSubscriptionModel`, `DcbSubscriptionModel`), and
`RepositionableSubscriptions`. `findIn` keeps calling `capability(type)` and follows the same rule.

A wrapper that keeps state for a subscription is then never bypassed by default. A wrapper is found for an acting
capability by implementing it, and its implementation updates its own state before forwarding.

The rule goes in the default method rather than in a `capability` override on each wrapper that keeps state. Overrides
on `CompetingConsumerSubscriptionModel` and `ManualStartSubscriptionModel` would fix the two shipped wrappers and leave
the same lookup going around every wrapper written later, in Occurrent or in an application.

### 2. `CompetingConsumerSubscriptionModel` answers empty for `RepositionableSubscriptions`

This follows from decision 1 with no code in `CompetingConsumerSubscriptionModel`. A resume at a position through a
competing consumer has to decide what a node without the lease does, and [ADR 134](0134-a-saga-instance-that-keeps-failing-is-quarantined-at-its-own-position.md)
decision 7 names the same question as open work for releasing a quarantined saga across nodes. Both get one answer, in
#1304. Going from empty to an implementation later adds a capability and breaks no caller.

### 3. `DurableSubscriptionModel` implements `RepositionableSubscriptions`

`resumeSubscription(subscriptionId, startAt)` stores the position and then resumes the wrapped model at it. The whole
call holds the lock `DurableSubscriptionModel` already takes per subscription id for its plain `resumeSubscription`.

* A subscription subscribed without checkpointing is forwarded to the wrapped model and nothing is stored.
* A subscription the wrapped model doesn't report as paused is forwarded too, and nothing is stored. The wrapped model
  then throws its own exception for an id it doesn't know or one that is already running, and no checkpoint is stored
  for either.
* `StartAt.checkpoint(..)` stores that checkpoint, then resumes there.
* `StartAt.now()` asks the wrapped model's `globalCheckpoint()` for the current position, stores it, then resumes
  there, so the stored and the actual start agree. When the wrapped model answers `null`, nothing is stored, the
  subscription stays paused and the call throws `IllegalStateException`.
* `StartAt.subscriptionModelDefault()` does what the plain `resumeSubscription(subscriptionId)` does, since the stored
  checkpoint is this model's default.
* A dynamic `StartAt` is resolved once and then handled as above. One that resolves to `null` throws
  `IllegalArgumentException`.
* A checkpoint the wrapped model can't subscribe at is forwarded to the wrapped model and nothing is stored. A restart
  subscribes the wrapped model at the stored checkpoint. A MongoDB model refuses a `GlobalCheckpoint` or a
  `CatchupTimeCheckpoint` there, and opens at the present for a time or one an application made up. Storing it would
  make a restart stop, or skip the events written in between.

The durable model can't tell those checkpoints apart itself, because only the wrapped model knows what it can open at.
So blocking `RepositionableSubscriptions` gets a default method, `restartsAt(Checkpoint)`, that answers `false`. The
MongoDB models override it and answer `true` for every checkpoint their change stream can open at, and the durable
model stores a position only when the wrapped model answers `true`. A wrong `false` makes a restart resume from the
checkpoint stored before, which delivers events again, and a wrong `true` makes it skip events, so a model that doesn't
override the method has nothing stored, as in 0.34.0. The durable model answers what its wrapped model answers. The
reactor `RepositionableSubscriptions` doesn't get the method, because `ReactorDurableSubscriptionModel` stores nothing
on a resume at a position.

The store comes first. The subscription is paused and the id lock is held, so no event's checkpoint can be written in
between. Resuming first would let an event's checkpoint be written and then overwritten with an older position.
Resuming first and then storing only when the stored checkpoint is still the one read before would avoid that, but
`CheckpointWriteCondition` has no such case. It has `any()`, `notOlderThan(..)` and `ifAbsent()`, and a fourth case
would have to be evaluated by every `CheckpointStorage`, the four Occurrent ships and every one an application wrote.

The store uses the same write condition as every other checkpoint write in the model (ADR 116, ADR 139). A refused
write throws `CheckpointWriteConditionNotFulfilledException`, nothing is resumed and the subscription stays paused,
because a node another node has fenced out must not move the position.

When the wrapped resume throws after the store, the model puts back the checkpoint stored before, under the same lock
and with the write condition the new position was stored with, and the exception propagates. A checkpoint another
lease holder wrote in the meantime then refuses the put-back. A failed reposition leaves the stored position as it
was before the call. A catch-up model that shares the checkpoint storage, as it does in the Spring Boot starter, replays
from the stored checkpoint. Had the new position stayed, a later resume would make the catch-up model go live at it
and skip the events written between its replay position and the new one. The MongoDB models pause the subscription
again before they throw, so no event was delivered from the new position when the old checkpoint goes back. A failure
to put the checkpoint back is added to the thrown exception as a suppressed exception.

When nothing was stored before, the new checkpoint stays. Deleting it could remove a checkpoint that another node, or
the resumed subscription's own events, wrote in the meantime. With nothing stored, a restart subscribes the wrapped
model at its default, which for the MongoDB models is the present.

`capability(RepositionableSubscriptions.class)` on a `DurableSubscriptionModel` answers the model itself when the
wrapped model can reposition and empty otherwise, as `ReactorDurableSubscriptionModel` and the catch-up models already
do. `resumeSubscription(subscriptionId, startAt)` throws `UnsupportedOperationException` when the wrapped model can't.

## Consequences

* `RepositionableSubscriptions.findIn(..)` on a `CompetingConsumerSubscriptionModel` or a
  `ManualStartSubscriptionModel` answers empty. In 0.33.0 and 0.34.0 it answered the model beneath. There is no way to
  resume a competing-consumer subscription at a position until #1304 is done. Over a `DurableSubscriptionModel`,
  pausing through the competing consumer and resuming through it starts from the stored checkpoint.
* `RepositionableSubscriptions.findIn(..)` on a `DurableSubscriptionModel` answers the durable model, and a resume at
  a position through it stores the checkpoint first, unless the wrapped model's `restartsAt(..)` answers
  `false` for it. A catch-up model over a durable model therefore stores the position at each live hand-over
  it repositions, which is the position it already stores for itself when both share one checkpoint storage, as they
  do in the Spring Boot starter.
* `capability(..)` for `Subscribable`, `CancellableSubscriptions` or a model type built on them answers empty on a
  wrapper that doesn't implement it, where it used to answer the model beneath.
* A `SubscriptionModelWrapper` of an application's own that should be found for an acting capability has to implement
  it. Observing capabilities are still found through it.
* ADR 119 called these lookups purely additive because they hadn't shipped. They shipped in 0.33.0, so this is a
  breaking change, with a changelog entry and a section in the 0.35.0 upgrade guide. The only new method is a default one,
  so there is no OpenRewrite recipe.
* A `DurableSubscriptionModel` over a repositionable subscription model of an application's own stores nothing on a
  resume at a position, as in 0.34.0, until that model overrides `restartsAt(..)` to answer `true` for the
  checkpoints it starts reading at.
* No stored document changes format. The `DurableSubscriptionModel` writes the same checkpoint with the same write

adrs.text:
# 132. An append has an identity, and read-your-writes becomes a membership question

Date: 2026-08-17

## Status

Accepted. Builds the design [ADR 122](0122-an-applied-position-is-not-a-completed-prefix.md) recorded as the
direction it could not build, and defines the implementation that
[#740](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/740) tracks. This ADR decides a design and writes no code.
The implementation is epic scale and reaches the cloud event extension, all four event stores, both result records,
`EventMetadata`, the projection DSL on both stacks, both Mongo starters, and the TCK.

[#361](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/361), which ADR 122 reopened, closes when that
implementation ships, and it closes on different terms than it asked for. It requests a wait for a projection
having applied every event up to a global position, which is the mechanism ADR 122 refuted. What ships instead
answers whether a projection has applied a named append, and decision 10 states where that is weaker. The goal
#361 describes is met and the mechanism it names is not built.

Corrected by [ADR 159](0159-six-passages-in-released-adrs-do-not-describe-the-code.md). The Consequences sentence
saying the blocking stacks filled no cache from history is true of the three blocking position catch-up stacks and not
of `BlockingHandover`, and decision 5 does not mention that the reactive Mongo store refuses a wait on a non-blocking
thread before its first read.

Amended by [ADR 166](0166-a-now-start-asks-to-replay-unless-it-starts-at-the-present-on-every-start.md). Decision 9's
third case holds for `NOW` only with `resumeBehavior = SAME_AS_START_AT`, for an unset `startAt` only for a stream or
an agnostic projection on the blocking stack, and for neither while a `SubscriptionResumePoints` bean is declared.

## Context

A caller that has just written wants to know when an asynchronous projection has applied that write.
[ADR 111](0111-a-projection-records-the-position-it-has-applied.md) answered it by recording the position a
projection had applied and waiting for that value to pass the caller's position. ADR 122 withdrew the feature,
because a position on MongoDB is reserved before commit while a change stream delivers in commit order
([ADR 84](0084-what-a-position-guarantees.md)), so a recorded maximum claims events that have not arrived yet.

That is settled, and this ADR does not reopen it. Nothing below reasons about the order events are delivered in,
about contiguity, or about how far a projection has got. ADR 122 is the binding refutation of that whole family.

### The question changes shape

ADR 122 named the replacement without building it. Mint one identifier per append, stamp it on every event of that
append the way `OccurrentCloudEventExtension` already stamps a position, return it from `WriteResult` and
`DcbAppendResult`, and have a projection record which identifiers it has applied. The wait then asks whether this
particular projection has already applied this particular append, which is a question about membership of a set
rather than about a position on a line.

Membership is answerable where the position question is not, for two reasons. It assumes nothing about the order
events arrive in. The case that broke the position design, where a writer reserves position 471 and stalls while a
writer holding 500 commits ahead of it, does nothing to a membership answer, because the wait asks about the
stalled writer's own append rather than about anything that overtook it.

The second reason is filtering. A subscription whose filter is pushed server-side into the change stream can still
answer the membership question, because a projection does not need to have seen the events it filtered out to know
which appends it applied.

The same design ports unchanged to a future PostgreSQL or MySQL store, where `BIGSERIAL` and `AUTO_INCREMENT` are
non-transactional for the same reason MongoDB's counter is and produce the identical mismatch between position and
commit order.

### What a replay does to a record of membership

A projection that replays the event store from the beginning would otherwise record every historical append
identifier it meets, and three separate things go wrong when it does.

The first is volume. A full replay over a large store inserts one membership record per handled event for no
benefit, since a replay is exactly the period when the projection has nothing useful to answer.

The second is that a replayed update returning does not mean the read model changed.
`CoalescingMaterializedView` buffers updates in memory while a replay runs, writing a batch out whenever the buffer
reaches its batch size and again when the replay completes (`CoalescingMaterializedView.java:90-95`, `:107-110`).
An abandoned replay discards whatever has not been written yet (`:113-117`). So an identifier recorded when the
delegate's update returned would, for every event still in that buffer, describe state nothing ever wrote.

The third is rebuilds. `CancellableSubscriptions` discards the checkpoint by contract, and
`ProjectionAnnotationRegistrar` backfills a new or rebuilt projection from the event store. Membership records
keyed by projection identifier alone outlive that rebuild, so a wait would answer `true` about a read model that
was wiped and is being built again from scratch.

### What each stack can be asked about its own replay

`ReplayAwareSubscriptions.isCatchingUp(subscriptionId)` already answers whether a subscription is still replaying,
and `SagaAnnotationRegistrar.java:235` already builds `isRunning(id) && !isCatchingUp(id)` to hold a saga's timers
back until the handover. So the question this design needs is one the library already asks in production, and no
new catch-up machinery is required. What it needs is a way to reach the model that can answer.

The saga asks it on its timer poll rather than per delivery, since `SagaRunner` evaluates that supplier inside the
task it hands to `scheduleWithFixedDelay`. This design asks per delivery instead, which is a higher frequency than
the existing precedent, and that is affordable because the answer is a lookup in a map the catch-up model keeps in
memory (`AbstractCatchupSubscriptionModel.java:144-148`) rather than a read from any store.

The two stacks differ there, and the difference decides part of this design. Blocking
`SubscriptionModelCapability.capability(Class)` unwraps a `SubscriptionModelWrapper` chain until it finds the
capability (`SubscriptionModelCapability.java:50-57`), so a lookup reaches an inner catch-up model however many
wrappers are in front of it. The reactor version is a direct `instanceof` against the object handed to it and says
so in its own javadoc (`SubscriptionModelCapability.java:37-47`), because that stack has no wrapper type to unwrap.

The default reactive Mongo composition is arranged so that difference matters.
`OccurrentReactiveMongoAutoConfiguration.occurrentDurableSubscriptionModel` marks a
`ReactorDurableSubscriptionModel` as `@Primary` and gives it `composeCatchupLayer(...)` to wrap, so a real
`ReactorCatchupSubscriptionModel` is running one level in. `ReactorDurableSubscriptionModel` implements
`CheckpointAwareSubscriptionModel`, `SubscriptionModel` and `IntrospectableSubscriptions`, but not
`ReplayAwareSubscriptions`. Asking that bean whether it is replaying answers empty, and empty means the model
cannot say, which reads the same as a model that never replays.

A design that decided by asking the model alone would therefore treat the standard reactive wiring as one that
never replays, and record straight through a genuine replay. That is the exact untruth this design exists to
prevent, so decision 8 does not ask the model alone.
[#842](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/842) tracks closing that difference between the stacks.

## Decision

### 1. `AppendId` is a value type, and the event store API owns it

`AppendId` is a value type wrapping a fresh UUID, never a bare `String` or `long`. This is the principle
[ADR 21](0021-dcb-write-path-query-scoped-concurrency.md) applied on the DCB write path, and ADR 122 identified a
`waitUntilApplied(String, long, Duration)` signature as repeating the mistake ADR 21 built a type-level guard
against.

It lives in `eventstore/api/common`, package `org.occurrent.eventstore.api`, beside `WriteResult`. The owner is
argued on what defines the concept, not on which module happens to reach it. An append identifier is minted by a
store inside a write or append call, and what it means is defined entirely by that operation. `DcbConsistencyToken`
is the closest existing thing, a value type a store hands back, living beside the result it is returned with.

The alternative was `cloudevents-extension`, and it is worth saying what it would buy, because reachability alone
argues for it. Both event store API modules already depend on that module, so an `AppendId` there could be returned
from a typed `EventMetadata` accessor directly. Against that, `cloudevents-extension` describes how Occurrent
stamps a CloudEvent and contains `EventMetadata`, `OccurrentCloudEventExtension` and two helpers, and no value type
at all. Putting `AppendId` there would make the module that defines the wire format also define what an append is,
which is the wrong way round. Deciding placement by which module can already reach a type is how a concept ends up
owned by whatever happened to import it first, so the placement is decided on ownership instead.

`eventstore/api/dcb` depends on `eventstore/api/common`, so `DcbAppendResult` reaches the type, and
`dsl/projection-dsl/common` already depends on `occurrent-eventstore-api-dcb`, so the projection layer reaches it
with no new dependency edge.

The extension key stays on `OccurrentCloudEventExtension` regardless of where the type lives, next to
`STREAM_ID`, `STREAM_VERSION` and `POSITION`.

Two readers exist rather than one. `EventMetadata` gains `getAppendId()` returning a nullable `String`, nullable
for the same reason `getPosition()` on that class is, so a caller holding metadata asks it directly instead of
routing through another type. `AppendId.from(EventMetadata)` returns an `Optional<AppendId>` and lives with `AppendId`, so
both stacks' recorders share one decision about what a missing extension means instead of writing that null check
twice.

### 2. The key is `appendid`, and stamping does not depend on `streamPositionEnabled`

The extension key is `appendid`, following the lowercase unseparated form of `streamid`, `streamversion` and
`position`. A write or append call that persists at least one event mints one identifier, and every event that call
persists is stamped with it. A call that persists nothing mints none, which is what decision 4 rests on.

Stamping happens in each store's own per-append loop, and not in
`OccurrentCloudEventMongoDocumentMapper.convertToDocument`, which is called per event and knows nothing about the
call it belongs to. Each of the four stores therefore stamps in its own code, on both the stream path and the DCB
path, and the two in-memory stamping methods already run under `synchronized(state)`.

Stamping is unconditional. `streamPositionEnabled`
(`eventstore/mongodb/native/.../nativedriver/EventStoreConfig.java:62`) governs whether the stream path
stamps a position, and an append identifier is not a position, so an application that turned position stamping off
still gets read-your-writes. Making the identifier depend on that setting would disable the feature through a
setting that names something else.

`updateEvent` keeps the identifier already stored on the event. `MongoEventStore.updateCloudEvent`
(`MongoEventStore.java:739`) calls the same `convertToDocument` the write path uses, and that path rewrites an event
that was persisted by some earlier append. Restamping it would move an event out of the append it belongs to and
into an append that never happened, so the stored valu

adrs.title: A NOW start asks to replay unless it starts at the present on every start
adrs.author: Johan Haleby
adrs.status_raw: Accepted. Amends decision 9 of [ADR 132](0132-an-append-has-an-identity-and-read-your-writes-becomes-a-membership-question.md), which shipped in 0.34.0 and is therefore amended by reference rather than edited. Part of [#1404](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1404).
adrs.text:
# 166. A NOW start asks to replay unless it starts at the present on every start

Date: 2026-11-05

## Status

Accepted. Amends decision 9 of [ADR 132](0132-an-append-has-an-identity-and-read-your-writes-becomes-a-membership-question.md),
which shipped in 0.34.0 and is therefore amended by reference rather than edited. Part of
[#1404](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1404).

## Context

Decision 9 of ADR 132 names a third composition that records with no automatic clear. It can replay and can report its
phase, but is wired so it is never asked to. It says `StartPosition.DEFAULT` with no global start position
set and `NOW` both put a catch-up-capable composition there, "since neither ever asks it to replay". Both starters'
`ProjectionAnnotationRegistrar` built a startup warning on that sentence, for a `recordAppliedAppends = true`
projection. The blocking one logged that recording never resets for every `startAt = NOW`, and for an unset
`startAt` on the MongoDB composition the starter configures. The reactive one logged it for `NOW` and for an unset
`startAt` on that composition.

The sentence is not true of `NOW` with the default `resumeBehavior`. On a restart such a subscription continues from
the checkpoint it stored, and when a catch-up stored that checkpoint, the catch-up replays from it. A projection whose
annotation went from `startAt = BEGINNING` to `startAt = NOW` between two deployments, after a catch-up that did not
finish, replays on the next boot. On the reactive stack an unset `startAt` starts the same way and replays too. The
registrar cannot know which kind of checkpoint a later boot finds, so it cannot promise that the projection never
replays.

On the blocking stack an unset `startAt` on a `@DcbSubscription`, a DCB `@Snapshot` or a DCB projection reaches the
catch-up layer as the model default, so it resumes from such a checkpoint and replays too. On a blocking stream or
agnostic subscription an unset `startAt` does not replay from such a checkpoint. It starts at the present instead, and
misses what was written while the application was down. That is a separate defect, older than 0.35.0, and this ADR
does not change it.

On the blocking stack, `NOW` with `resumeBehavior = SAME_AS_START_AT` keeps no position on Occurrent's durable and
competing consumer models. A restart with a catch-up checkpoint in storage gets only the event written after it
started. A pause and a resume replayed, because the catch-up layer read the checkpoint on the resume. On the reactive
stack a resume with a catch-up checkpoint in storage does not replay from it.

A `SubscriptionResumePoints` bean, new in 0.35.0, can replace the start an annotation built with a checkpoint, `NOW`
and `DEFAULT` alike.

## Decision

Decision 9's third case covers `NOW` only with `resumeBehavior = SAME_AS_START_AT`. `NOW` with the default
`resumeBehavior` is a start that can ask its composition to replay, and it records and clears the way any replaying
start does. On the reactive stack an unset `startAt` is such a start too, and it is no longer in the third case. On the
blocking stack it stays there for a stream or an agnostic projection, since that never replays. A DCB projection
with `startAt` unset is no longer in it.

With no `SubscriptionResumePoints` bean answering for it, `NOW` with `SAME_AS_START_AT` starts at the present on every
restart, and a resume doesn't replay from a catch-up checkpoint in storage. On the blocking stack it bypasses the
catch-up layer as well as the durable and competing consumer ones, so without such a bean no layer reads a position
for it.

Neither `NOW` nor `DEFAULT` belongs to the third case when the application declares a `SubscriptionResumePoints`
bean.

Both registrars' warnings follow this. A push projection with `catchup = NONE` still warns on both stacks, whatever
beans are declared, since the bean doesn't start it. For a projection that subscribes to the event store:

- The blocking one fires for `NOW` only with `SAME_AS_START_AT`, and for an unset `startAt` on a stream or an
  agnostic projection on the composition the starter configures. It doesn't fire while a `SubscriptionResumePoints`
  bean is declared.
- The reactive one fires for `NOW` only with `SAME_AS_START_AT`, and for a composition with no catch-up layer. With
  a `SubscriptionResumePoints` bean declared it fires only for a composition with no catch-up layer, which never
  replays whatever the start.

## Consequences

- A `NOW` projection with the default `resumeBehavior` no longer gets a warning that was false whenever a catch-up
  checkpoint was stored for it. When no such checkpoint is stored it does not replay either, and it now starts without
  the warning that would have been true. The registrar cannot tell the two apart at startup. The same holds for a
  reactive projection, and a blocking DCB projection, with `startAt` unset.
- `ComposedCatchupModel.defaultBypassesCatchup` still records that a first start with `startAt` unset doesn't replay,
  but the reactive warning no longer reads it.
- On the blocking stack the warning for `NOW` with `SAME_AS_START_AT` rests on Occurrent's own models opting out of
  keeping a position. On the reactive stack it rests on tests of the stream composition the starter configures. In both,
  an application-supplied model of another type that keeps a position is not seen by the registrar.
- An application that declares a `SubscriptionResumePoints` bean gets the warning only for a push projection with
  `catchup = NONE` and, on the reactive stack, for a composition with no catch-up layer. That holds even for a
  projection whose resume points never answer a checkpoint. The registrar does not ask the bean, since its answer can
  change from one start to the next.
- If the blocking defect with an unset `startAt` is fixed by resuming from the catch-up checkpoint, that start
  replays, and the blocking warning for it has to go the way the reactive one did.

adrs.title: A Spring Mongo transaction manager sends a commit again when its result is unknown
adrs.author: Johan Haleby
adrs.status_raw: Accepted. Resolves [#1384](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1384).
adrs.text:
# 163. A Spring Mongo transaction manager sends a commit again when its result is unknown

Date: 2026-10-30

## Status

Accepted. Resolves [#1384](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1384).

## Context

MongoDB marks a commit it could not answer with the error label `UnknownTransactionCommitResult`. The commit reached
the server, or may have, and the reply was lost, for example to a network error or to a primary that stepped down. The
transaction is then committed or not, and the MongoDB documentation says to send `commitTransaction` again. The driver
accepts that on the same session.

The native `MongoEventStore` runs its transaction through `ClientSession.withTransaction`, which does so for up to 120
seconds. `SpringMongoEventStore` and `ReactorMongoEventStore` run it through Spring's `MongoTransactionManager` and
`ReactiveMongoTransactionManager`, and neither sends a commit again. Spring turns the failure into a
`TransactionSystemException` that holds the `MongoException` with its label, and no code in either store looks at it.
The stores' own retry looks for the `TransientTransactionError` label and for a duplicate key, not for this label.

An append that may have been saved is therefore reported to the caller as a failure. If the caller sends it again with
new event ids, the events can be written twice. If it sends the same ids, the unique `(id, source)` index refuses them
as a `DuplicateCloudEventException`, for events that are stored.

## Decision

Occurrent ships `CommitRetryingMongoTransactionManager` and `CommitRetryingReactiveMongoTransactionManager`. Each
extends Spring's manager and overrides the protected `doCommit`, which Spring documents as the place to retry a commit.
The retry follows the driver's `withTransaction`:

- It retries a commit that fails with the `UnknownTransactionCommitResult` label, found on the first `MongoException`
  in the cause chain of the failure.
- It does not retry a top-level `MaxTimeMSExpired` error (`MongoExecutionTimeoutException`) or
  `MongoOperationTimeoutException`, which the driver does not retry either. A write concern error with the
  `MaxTimeMSExpired` code (50) reaches the manager as the same `MongoExecutionTimeoutException`, because the driver
  raises it that way, so it is not retried either. Against a MongoDB replica set with a fail point, both stacks sent one
  commit and the event was stored.
- It stops retrying 120 seconds after the first commit was sent, and throws or emits the last error. The number is the
  driver's `MAX_RETRY_TIME_LIMIT_MS`, but the driver counts it from the start of its `withTransaction` call, before the
  transaction body runs, so the driver's window can be shorter than ours by the time the body takes. The caller sees the same failure it sees today, and the append may or may not be saved.
- It does not share a `timeoutMS` across the resends the way `withTransaction` does, because Spring calls the plain
  `commitTransaction()`, so with `timeoutMS` configured each resend gets a fresh timeout and the 120 seconds still
  end the retry.
- It checks the time between attempts, as the driver does, so a commit that has started is not interrupted and ends on
  the driver's own timeouts.
- It sends the next commit at once, as the driver does. The second `commitTransaction` call on the same session is the
  one that makes the driver send the commit with a majority write concern, so the resend is not acknowledged by the
  primary alone, whatever write concern the transaction started with.

Both Spring Boot starters create these managers instead of the plain ones. They still back off when the application
defines its own `MongoTransactionManager` or `ReactiveMongoTransactionManager`, and the blocking one still passes the
majority read and write concern as transaction options.

A `SpringMongoEventStore` whose transaction manager is not a `CommitRetryingMongoTransactionManager` logs one warning
when it is created. The reactive store's `EventStoreConfig.Builder.transactionConfig(ReactiveTransactionManager)` does
the same. `transactionConfig(TransactionalOperator)` can't, because a `TransactionalOperator` does not expose the
manager it came from, so an application that passes an operator gets no warning. The migration guide says so.

The store does not retry the commit itself. By the time Spring has translated the failure, the store would have to run
the whole append again, and an append that was in fact saved would be reported as a failure, because the same event
ids are refused by the unique `(id, source)` index. Retrying only the commit is correct because the transaction is
already complete on the session.

Running the transaction through `ClientSession.withTransaction` was considered and rejected. It bypasses the
`TransactionTemplate` the user configured, and the reactive driver has no such method.

## Consequences

- A commit whose result is unknown is sent again for up to two minutes. Its append is reported as written when the
  second commit succeeds, and it is written once.
- An application that wires the store by hand must switch its transaction manager to get the retry. The warning
  tells it so, and the migration guide to 0.35.0 shows the change. The examples in this repository were switched.
- When the store joins a transaction the caller started, the commit belongs to the caller's manager, so the retry
  happens only if that manager is one of these two. The tests cover both a retrying and a plain manager for that case.
- The two classes are public API in `occurrent-eventstore-mongodb-spring-blocking` and
  `occurrent-eventstore-mongodb-spring-reactor`. The decision of what counts as retryable lives in an internal class in
  `occurrent-eventstore-mongodb-common`, so the two stacks cannot drift apart.

adrs.text:
# 21. DCB write-path query-scoped concurrency

Date: 2026-06-22

## Status

Accepted. Amended by [ADR 148](0148-dcb-snapshots-resume-from-marker-versions-not-positions.md) on pruning. A pruned marker is
recreated with a new epoch, so pruning also invalidates every DCB snapshot on that boundary. The read refuses such a
snapshot, and it's rebuilt from a full read on its next use.

Amended by [ADR 149](0149-the-mongodb-dcb-append-check-compares-each-marker-and-then-the-events-above-it.md) on pruning and on how the check compares a token. A token now holds what the read saw of each
marker, so the check compares each marker, not a sum. The operator guidance under Consequences no longer holds. A
marker may be deleted only in a transaction that also finds no event with its tag or type.

Amended by [ADR 147](0147-a-dcb-consistency-token-belongs-to-the-criteria-it-was-read-with.md). For a criteria item with at least one tag, the query reads and increments only its `tag:`
markers and no longer its `type:` markers, so sharing a type with such an item is no longer a reason for the check to
refuse. What an append increments for its own events is unchanged, so two
appends of one type that run at the same time still write the same `type:` marker.

Amended by [ADR 164](0164-a-spring-mongo-dcb-append-retries-a-transaction-conflict-for-about-two-minutes.md). "Contention surfaces as a retry, not a spurious command failure" holds while an append loses fewer than 240 attempts in a row on the blocking store, or 321 on the reactive one, within about two minutes of waiting. An append that loses every attempt fails with the last error.

## Context

`SpringMongoEventStore.appendDcb` appends DCB events under an optional `DcbAppendCondition`, which is the DCB optimistic-concurrency check: fail the append if any event matching the condition's `DcbQuery` exists after the position the command read. The current implementation has three concurrency problems.

1. Every append reserves its global `dcbposition` block with a `findAndModify` `$inc` on a single counter document, inside the append transaction. Under concurrency that one document is a hot spot. Concurrent appends contend on it and MongoDB raises a `TransientTransactionError`, which aborts the whole transaction.

2. There is no retry for transient transaction errors. `MongoTransactionManager` does not retry them, and the only retry in play is the application service retrying `DcbAppendConditionNotFulfilledException`. So contention surfaces as a spurious command failure rather than a retry.

3. The conflict-serialization keying is not skew-safe. The append writes per-key checkpoint documents to force concurrent appends on the same boundary to conflict, but it keys a tag item as `tag:<tag>` and a type-only item as `type:<type>`. Two overlapping queries that match the same event by different dimensions, for example `types(X)` and `tagsAllOf("t")` both matching an event `{type:X, tag:t}`, get disjoint keys, so they do not conflict. Today the global counter serialization in problem 1 hides this, because every append contends on the counter anyway. Remove that serialization for scalability and write skew becomes possible: two commands each read a boundary, each append a matching event, and both commit even though the second should have failed.

The goal is query-scoped concurrency. Appends to disjoint boundaries proceed in parallel, appends to the same boundary serialize, and no pair of appends that can match a common event is ever allowed to both commit when one should fail.

## Decision

### Assign positions outside the transaction

Move the `dcbposition` counter `findAndModify` out of the append transaction. It is a single atomic update, which MongoDB serializes efficiently at the document level without raising a transaction conflict. The reserved block is reused if the transaction is retried, and is simply abandoned if the append fails its condition. `dcbposition` stays strictly increasing but may have gaps, which the DCB contract permits (ADR 0017). The unique sparse index on `dcbposition` still guarantees no two events share a position.

### Detect and serialize conflicts with versioned per-attribute markers

Assigning positions outside the transaction has a consequence: a reader can observe a global head that runs ahead of the data it can see, because a concurrent append reserves its position block before it commits. A conflict check phrased over positions ("fail if a matching event exists after the position I read") is therefore unsound. The reader's boundary can sit past an append that is still in flight, which then commits at a position at or below that boundary and is never seen, so the conflict is lost silently. The conflict check must not depend on positions.

Instead, every distinct tag and type has a marker document carrying a monotonically increasing version. An append derives its marker keys from per-attribute units, never combined:

- For a tag `t`, the key `tag:t`.
- For a type `X`, the key `type:X`.

Inside the transaction the append increments the marker version for the union of:

- the appended events' keys (every tag and the type of each appended event), on every append whether or not it carries a condition, and
- the condition query's keys when a condition is present (every tag and every included type named by any query item).

Incrementing a shared marker document forces a write-write conflict in MongoDB, so two transactions that touch a common marker cannot both commit. The sharing argument is unchanged: if append A1 commits an event E1 that matches append A2's query Q2, then some item of Q2 is satisfied by E1, so A1 touches that item's `tag:t` or `type:X` marker from its event keys and A2 touches the same marker from its query keys, and the two serialize. The reverse direction (E2 matching Q1) holds by the same argument. Because an unconditional append also increments its events' markers, it cannot slip past a concurrent conditional append on an overlapping tag or type.

A read captures a consistency token for its query: the sum of the versions of the query's markers. Versions are incremented at commit and never at reservation, so the token reflects only committed appends and is immune to the position overshoot above. The authoritative conflict check compares the token the condition carries against the current token inside the transaction. If any of the query's markers advanced since the read, a matching append committed in between, so the condition fails. The marker increments still force serialization, so the loser re-runs this comparison against the winner's committed increment rather than racing it under snapshot isolation.

The token is distinct from the read's `lastSequencePosition`. The position remains a global cursor for replay and catch-up. The token is the optimistic-concurrency boundary, and the two are different types (`DcbConsistencyToken` versus `long`) so a caller cannot pass one where the other is required.

### Retry transient transaction errors

Wrap the append transaction in a bounded retry that recognises MongoDB transient transaction errors (the `TransientTransactionError` error label, surfaced by Spring as `UncategorizedMongoDbException` / `MongoException.hasErrorLabel`). On retry the reserved position block is reused and the condition is re-evaluated, so a retry either commits or fails the condition correctly. `DcbAppendConditionNotFulfilledException` is not retried here, it propagates to the application service, which re-reads and retries the command.

### A MatchAll condition is a whole-store lock

A `MatchAll` condition matches every event, so no per-attribute marker can be shared with an arbitrary concurrent append without making every append write a single global marker, which is global serialization. A `MatchAll` append condition is therefore a whole-store optimistic lock keyed `all`: it is skew-safe against other `MatchAll` conditions, but it is NOT skew-safe against a concurrent tag-scoped or type-scoped append (the two share no marker, so both can commit even when the `MatchAll` condition should have failed). This is a correctness limitation under concurrency, not merely a performance one, so a `MatchAll` append condition must not be relied on as a consistency boundary on a store that takes concurrent writes. It is fine on a single-writer store or as a one-shot "the store is empty" guard. Tag-scoped and type-scoped boundaries, the normal DCB usage, are fully skew-safe.

A query item with neither types nor tags cannot be constructed (`DcbQueryItem` rejects it), so there is no separate negative-only or empty-item case to reason about. An item always carries at least one positive tag or type, which is what makes its marker shareable. Excluded types only narrow a positive item and never remove its positive marker keys, so they do not affect skew-safety. They do reduce precision: see the over-approximation note in the consequences.

## Consequences

Positive:

- Appends to disjoint boundaries no longer contend on a global counter or a global checkpoint, so they scale concurrently.
- The conflict keying is skew-safe for tag-scoped and type-scoped boundaries, proven against the type-versus-tag, tag-versus-tag, and type-versus-type overlap cases by adversarial multi-threaded tests.
- Contention surfaces as a retry, not a spurious command failure.
- The conflict check is a lookup of the query's marker documents by `_id`, which is always index-backed, and the read query is index-backed by the `dcbtags` and `dcbposition` indexes, confirmed with `explain`.
- The conflict check is decoupled from positions, so it is sound even though positions are assigned outside the transaction and the read head can run ahead of committed data.

Negative:

- `dcbposition` can have gaps, because a reserved block is abandoned when an append fails its condition or exhausts its transient retries. DCB only requires monotonic increasing positions, so gaps are acceptable, but callers must not assume contiguity (they already must not, per ADR 0017).
- The marker collection holds one document per distinct tag and per distinct type that has taken part in an append. For high-cardinality tags, for example a tag per entity, this is one marker per entity. That is the natural granularity of the consistency boundary and matches the cardinality the boundary already implies. Markers are not removed when an event stream is deleted, and there is no automatic reclamation. A marker only carries a version counter, so it is safe to drop a marker while no append that references it is in flight: the next append that touches that key recreates it with the upsert. An operator can therefore prune the checkpoint collection during quiescence if marker cardinality becomes a concern, at the cost of resetting those counters (which is harmless, because a reader's token is only ever compared against the same store's current value).
- A `MatchAll` or negative-only append condition is a whole-store lock as described above. This is a documented limitation, not a silent one.
- The token-based check is a safe over-approximation. It is derived from positive markers only, so it cannot represent excluded types or multi-attribute conjunctions precisely. An append of an excluded-type event that still carries a query's positive tag, or an append that carries only some of a conjunction's tags, advances a shared marker and conservatively conflicts even though it does not match the full query. This never misses a real conflict, reads still apply excluded types and conjunctions precisely, and the false conflict self-heals through the application service, which re-reads the still-filtered boundary and retries. The cost is reduced concurrency between appends on a shared tag or type, which is the boundary the caller chose.

adrs.text:
# 80. What concurrent writes to one stream guarantee

Date: 2026-07-30

## Status

Accepted. Adds `StreamConcurrencyConformance` to the TCK ([ADR 77](0077-a-published-tck-for-occurrent-contracts.md)) and
changes the reactive event store's write path, which has shipped. Resolves #467, #474 and #475.

Amended by [ADR 164](0164-a-spring-mongo-dcb-append-retries-a-transaction-conflict-for-about-two-minutes.md). The reactive
store's retry of a lost `any()` version race makes 320 retries now, not 15, so the 15-retry ceiling named below no
longer holds.

## Context

Optimistic concurrency is the reason an event store takes a `WriteCondition` at all, and until now it was the least
verified part of the write path.

Five tests covered it, all inside `ParallelWritesToEventStoreReturns` in the three MongoDB store test classes, and every
one of them carried `@EnabledOnOs(MAC)`. Every CI shard runs `ubuntu-latest`, so those five ran on one laptop and
nowhere else. The in-memory store had no such test at all.

Nothing records why the gate went on. Not a commit message, not `changelog.md`, not this repository's docs, not an issue
or a pull request. What survives is a sequence from 2021-04-16: the test arrived as a plain `@Test`, hours later it
became `@RepeatedIfExceptionsTest(repeats = 10)` under the message "Hopefully fixing race conditions in test", and hours
after that the gate appeared while repeats dropped to 5. A retry escalation that did not settle it, then a gate.

The premise a reader would assume, green on CI and red locally, is the wrong way round. CI in April 2021 was already
`ubuntu-latest` and already ran these tests under Surefire, so the gate excluded CI from the moment it was written. The
two later occurrences (2022 and 2024) copy the annotation from the sibling above them. The DCB concurrency tests use the
identical replica-set fixture, are not gated, and pass on Linux CI today.

Writing the suite then turned up two defects that the gate had been hiding, both fixed here.

`ReactorMongoEventStore.write` had no retry on a version race, so two concurrent writes under `anyStreamVersion()` could
leave one caller with a `WriteConditionNotFulfilledException` that the condition promises cannot happen. Both blocking
stores retry. Commit `fe99e0bdf` names only those two, so the reactive store was a known omission from October 2024
rather than an oversight here.

And the two DCB concurrency test classes joined `futA.get()` before `futB.get()`, so a throw from the first abandoned
the second join while `shutdown()` left that worker running. The test method then returned with a thread still appending
into a store the next class asserts on. Every wait in both files was unbounded, backed only by a class-level
`@Timeout(180)`, which reports a hang after three minutes without saying which worker wedged.

## Decision

State the contract in one place, assert it in the TCK against all four stores, and fix whatever fails.

**A conditional write from two threads leaves exactly one winner.** The loser gets
`WriteConditionNotFulfilledException` and writes nothing. Asserted on a count, not on `contains`, because `contains`
passes on a store that wrote both.

**An unconditional write does not fail on a version race, as long as the store keeps retrying through it.**
`anyStreamVersion()` means a write that loses a race retries rather than surfacing the conflict. The two blocking
Mongo stores retry with no fixed attempt limit, `RetryStrategy.retry()`'s default. The reactive store instead caps
the retry at 15 attempts with backoff, because retrying an unbounded reactive pipeline with neither a delay nor a
limit spins a scheduler thread. The suite's contention, 6 threads racing on one stream over 5 iterations, settles
well inside that 15-attempt cap, so every writer succeeds and every event is present exactly once on all four stores.
A stream contended past what the reactive store's 15 backed-off retries can clear still exhausts them and throws
there. The blocking stores have no such ceiling to hit.

The reactive store gets the retry the blocking ones have, routed through the existing
transaction-ownership check ([ADR 74](0074-retry-only-where-the-transaction-is-owned.md)) so it only retries a
transaction it opened.

### The in-memory guarantee comes from `Map.compute`, not from the surrounding block

Worth writing down, because the obvious reading is wrong and this was checked by breaking it rather than by reading it.

`InMemoryEventStore.write` holds `synchronized (state)` around a `state.compute` call. Removing that block does not
break exactly-one-winner: `state` is a `Collections.synchronizedMap`, where `compute` is already atomic on its own, and
the loser writes nothing because its `WriteConditionNotFulfilledException` is thrown from inside the remapping function,
before `compute` can install a value. The outer block is what makes the read-then-write of the position counter atomic
with the append, and in `delete(Filter)` it is what guards iterating a view of the map, which `compute` does not cover.

So the property that makes the suite pass is narrower than the code's shape suggests. A future reader trimming the
`synchronized` as redundant would keep this test green and break position assignment.

### Every wait in the TCK is bounded, because the shards have no retry

The barrier and every join take a timeout, every future is joined before anything is asserted, the pool is shut down
with `shutdownNow()`, and `ExecutionException` is unwrapped so an assertion sees the store's exception rather than the
executor's wrapper. The discipline is taken from `SpringMongoMaterializedViewConfigTest.kt`, which already had it.

This is not tidiness. The eventstore shards deliberately carry no `surefire.rerunFailingTestsCount`, so a flake there is
a red build rather than a silent second attempt, and a suite that hangs costs the shard's whole 20 minute timeout. The
same treatment goes to the two DCB classes, whose abandoned join is a live contamination source in CI today: its symptom
is a failure in an unrelated class, which is close to undiagnosable from a log.

### The gated tests are deleted rather than un-gated

They add nothing the build did not already have, since they ran on no CI platform, and they are weak where they did run.
Both racing threads write one `AtomicReference` with last-write-wins, no thread is joined, the any-version variants
assert `contains` rather than a count, and an Awaitility poll can only fail by timing out.

Three `@EnabledOnJre(JAVA_8)` tests go with them. The project targets 21, so they are dead rather than gated.

A script guards the class of problem instead of the instances: it parses `runs-on` and the `java:` matrix out of
`maven.yml`, parses `@EnabledOnOs` and `@EnabledOnJre` out of `src/test`, and fails naming any test no CI job can run.
It reads the workflow rather than keeping a second list, which is what makes `verify-shard-coverage` durable. Deleting
the eight instances is what lets the guard start from zero instead of shipping with an allow-list.

`SuiteNeverSkipsTest` covers the new suite too, since a grep cannot see an engine-level skip.

## Consequences

A concurrent unconditional write behaves the same on all four stores now, so code written against the blocking stores
ports to the reactive one without acquiring a failure mode. Only the reactive store caps its retry, at 15 attempts
with backoff up to 500ms, so a genuinely contended stream fails there eventually rather than never. The blocking
stores retry without that cap.

The suite runs 5 iterations per test and passes in under 5 seconds per store, well inside the 240 second shard budget.
`eventstore/mongodb/spring` is the shard to watch as the TCK grows: it is a single path carrying both the blocking and
the reactive store, so if it goes over budget there is nothing to move out of it.

The in-memory store's exactly-one-winner property is now asserted rather than incidental, which is the first test of
concurrent same-stream writes it has ever had.

An implementation outside this repository that cannot retry an any-version write cannot pass the suite. That is
deliberate: the alternative is a fixture flag recording the gap as an intended difference, which is the pattern #470
removed two instances of.

What this does not cover: DCB append concurrency, which the two DCB classes still own. Their waiting discipline is fixed
here because it is a live defect, but they already cover DCB thoroughly on Linux CI, so folding them into the TCK is
deduplication rather than coverage and belongs with the rest of the DCB phase.

adrs.text:
# 148. DCB snapshots resume from marker versions, not positions

Date: 2026-10-24

## Status

Accepted. Fixes [#1230](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1230) and settles the 0.35 contract for
[#1297](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1297). Applies to the three MongoDB event stores
(`SpringMongoEventStore`, `MongoEventStore` and `ReactorMongoEventStore`), `InMemoryEventStore`, the snapshot DSL on
both stacks and the DCB `@Snapshot` view. Amends [ADR 61](0061-first-class-snapshot-support.md), whose DCB snapshot
version is a position. Amends [ADR 21](0021-dcb-write-path-query-scoped-concurrency.md) on what pruning markers costs.
Extends [ADR 84](0084-what-a-position-guarantees.md) with what a position can't be used for.

## Context

### The defect

A MongoDB store that runs the append transaction itself reserves a block of positions before that transaction starts.
The reservation is one atomic `$inc` on a counter document, outside the transaction, in each store's `reservePositions`.
The block is reused when the transaction is retried. So an append can own a position for a long time before its events
are visible, and an append that reserved later can commit first.

[ADR 84](0084-what-a-position-guarantees.md) states this as the contract:

> **A position is not commit order.** Reservation happens before commit, so two concurrent writers can commit in the
> opposite order to their positions.

That's harmless for a reader that only sorts events. It loses events for a reader that stores the highest position it
has seen and later reads only what comes after it. Below, I call such a stored position a watermark.

[#1230](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1230) is the DCB case. Take the boundary
`types(Deposited, Withdrawn).tags(account:a1)`:

1. A deposit appends `Deposited(a1, 5)` without an append condition. It reserves position 41. Its first transaction
   attempt aborts on a transient error, and it backs off before it retries.
2. A withdraw runs `Withdraw(a1, 3)` through `SnapshotDcbDeciderApplicationService`. It reads the events after the old
   snapshot version, decides, reserves 42 and commits. Its append condition passes, because nothing matching had
   committed since its read.
3. The service saves the new snapshot with version 42, which is `DcbAppendResult.lastSequencePosition()`
   (`SnapshotDcbDeciderApplicationService.java:161`).
4. The deposit retries and commits at 41.
5. The next command reads with `fromPosition(42)` (`SnapshotDcbDeciderApplicationService.java:145`) and never gets 41.
   Its consistency token doesn't help, because 41 committed before that read.

From then on every decision on `account:a1` uses a balance that is 5 too low, and every later snapshot starts from that
state. A reproduction that holds one append between its reservation and its transaction ends with a balance of 7 where
12 is right. The reactive service saves the same way (`ReactiveSnapshotDcbDeciderApplicationService.java:166`, `:188`).

The DCB `@Snapshot` view has the same defect from the other side. It treats every delivered event at or below its saved
version as a redelivery (`SnapshotAnnotationRegistrar.java:186`), so the deposit at 41, delivered after the withdraw at
42, is skipped as if it had already been applied to the view's state.

[#1297](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1297) is the store-wide case, for catch-up subscriptions that
resume from a position:

1. A catch-up subscription reads past 42 while a stream write that reserved 41 is still delayed, and the application
   stores 42 as `GlobalCheckpoint.of(42)`.
2. The stream write commits at 41.
3. The application restarts and resumes from that checkpoint. The catch-up reads a new live start, which is the point in
   the change stream it will follow once the replay is done, and replays the events after 42.
4. The replay doesn't read 41, because 41 is below 42. The change stream doesn't deliver it either, because 41 committed
   before the new live start.

A catch-up that stored its live start together with the position
([ADR 144](0144-a-catch-up-checkpoint-keeps-the-live-start-it-read-before-the-replay.md)) doesn't have this problem,
because it keeps the live start the earlier attempt read before 41 committed. It happens when the position is stored
alone. That's a position the application stored itself, a checkpoint written by 0.34 or earlier, or a checkpoint stored
during a catch-up that only replays and never goes live.

[#1298](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1298) has the same defect in the saga position watermark. It's
fixed separately and this ADR doesn't change it.

The append condition is not affected. Its consistency token is the sum of the versions of marker documents that the
append increments inside its transaction ([ADR 21](0021-dcb-write-path-query-scoped-concurrency.md),
`MongoEventStore.java:524-550`, `:580-605`), not a position. ADR 21 already explained why a condition phrased over
positions is unsound. The snapshot decider and the view were written later and used a position as their version anyway.

### Designs we tried

Seven designs came before the decision. Each one is described with how it works, the interleaving that broke it or the
cost that ruled it out, and why I dropped it.

#### 1. Reserve the position outside the transaction (the behaviour this ADR fixes)

Before ADR 21, the DCB append reserved its block inside the transaction. Concurrent appends then all wrote the one
counter document, and MongoDB raised a `TransientTransactionError` that aborted the whole transaction. ADR 21 moved the
reservation out, so the counter became one atomic update that MongoDB serializes without a transaction conflict, and the
positions of a failed append are never used. [ADR 84](0084-what-a-position-guarantees.md) then wrote down what that
costs. A position is not commit order, and `currentPosition()` "is a high-watermark, not a fence".

ADR 21 replaced positions with marker versions for the append condition. The snapshot decider and the `@Snapshot` view
([ADR 61](0061-first-class-snapshot-support.md)) kept using a position as their version. ADR 61 even argued that a DCB
snapshot needs no check for being ahead of the head, because a DCB version "is a global, monotonic position that never
resets". That's true for the head of the store. The defect is a position below the version whose event isn't visible yet
when the snapshot is saved. The two walkthroughs above are what that costs.

#### 2. Re-read an overlap behind the saved position

The cheapest fix is to resume from the snapshot version minus some margin, say 100 positions, so a late commit just
below the version is still read.

That fails in two ways. The first is that no margin is long enough. The deposit reserves 41 and its process stalls (a
long GC pause, a network partition, a transaction stuck in its retries). 150 other appends commit meanwhile, and the
withdraw saves its snapshot at 192. The next command resumes from 92. The deposit then commits at 41, and every later
command misses it. The native store retries an append with the same block up to 15 times with backoff between 10 and 500 ms
(`MongoEventStore.java:664-669`), the Spring stores for about two minutes (ADR 164), and a paused process adds any
amount of time on top.

The second is that the snapshot state doesn't record which events it already applied. Resuming from 92 reads the events
at 93 to 192 again, and the decider applies them a second time. Fixing that needs a set of applied event ids in every
snapshot.

I dropped it because it makes the loss less likely without removing it, and I won't accept a design that can still lose
an event here.

#### 3. Reserve the position inside the transaction

If every append, DCB and stream, writes the counter inside its transaction, positions become commit order. A reader that
sees 42 then knows that 41 either committed before it or never will. Spring's outer-transaction mode worked this way in
0.34.0, since the counter update joined the caller's transaction there.

The cost is throughput under contention. Inside a transaction, MongoDB doesn't wait for a document another transaction
has modified. It aborts the second transaction with a `WriteConflict`. Outside a transaction the server retries the same
write internally until it succeeds, which is why today's counter is a busy document but not a source of aborts. So with
the reservation inside, appends A and B both start, A increments the counter, B's increment conflicts and B aborts into
the 10 to 500 ms backoff, and when B retries it may conflict with C. Roughly one append gets through per transaction
latency, and the rest spend their time in backoff. The design search (design 7 below) estimated a ceiling of tens to low
hundreds of appends per second. That estimate is reasoned from commit latency and not measured.

This is the contention ADR 21 removed, and it would also make every append in the store conflict with every other, not
only appends on the same boundary. I rejected it for performance.

#### 4. A complete-through position with an age rule

This was the first design that went through review, and the next three are revisions of it. The idea is a position the
store can promise, called the complete-through position or CT. It is the highest position below which every reserved
block has either committed or can never commit. A reader that only ever stores CT as its watermark can't miss a late
commit.

The store learns which blocks are still open like this:

- The counter document gets an `inflight` array next to `position`. The reservation becomes one pipeline
  `findOneAndUpdate` that increments `position` by n and appends `{last, n, at}` to `inflight` in the same write. An
  entry's first position is `last - n + 1`.
- A new fence collection holds one document per block, with the block's first position as its unique `_id` and a `kind`
  of `commit` or `abort`.
- The append transaction inserts the `commit` fence as its first write, so the fence commits with the events or not at
  all. Every failure exit inserts an `abort` fence outside the transaction. Once either fence exists the other can't be
  inserted, so a block with an `abort` fence can never commit.
- A reader reads the counter document, then the fences for the entries in `inflight`. CT is `first - 1` of the lowest
  entry without a fence, or `position` when every entry has one.
- An appender inserts an `abort` fence for an entry older than 120 seconds that still has no fence, so a crashed process
  can't keep CT down for ever.

The decider had to learn its own CT. A first version saved the snapshot when the CT read after its own commit had
reached its last position. The first review broke that. Append X reserves 41, its marker write loses the write conflict
against the withdraw, the withdraw commits at 42, X retries with the same block and commits at 41 after it. Then CT
reaches 42, and the withdraw saves at 42 without X's event. The fix read the counter and the fences inside the append
transaction, in the same snapshot as the append condition, and saved at the last position only when every entry below
its own block had a fence in that snapshot.

The second review removed a step that deleted the append's own entry with a `$pull` after commit. That doubled the
writes on the counter document, made appends in a caller's transaction conflict on it, and couldn't work in native
ambient mode, where the caller commits after `append` returns. It also found that the native store reserves outside the
caller's ambient transaction (`reservePositions` runs before the ambient session check).

Fences expired after an hour, so the fence collection wouldn't grow for ever. That hour comes from a draft I no longer
have, so it's unchecked. The third review found that once a fence expires, its entry looks open again. CT then drops
back below it, and on a quiet store a reader waits for ever. The
