adrs.author: Johan Haleby
adrs.status_raw: Accepted. Amends [ADR 21](0021-dcb-write-path-query-scoped-concurrency.md), [ADR 74](0074-retry-only-where-the-transaction-is-owned.md) and [ADR 80](0080-concurrent-write-conformance.md), which have shipped in a release and are therefore corrected here and not edited. ADR 74 says the executors match
adrs.text:
# 164. A Spring Mongo DCB append retries a transaction conflict for about two minutes

Date: 2026-10-30

## Status

Accepted. Amends [ADR 21](0021-dcb-write-path-query-scoped-concurrency.md), [ADR 74](0074-retry-only-where-the-transaction-is-owned.md)
and [ADR 80](0080-concurrent-write-conformance.md), which have shipped in a release and are therefore corrected here and not edited.
ADR 74 says the executors match `DataIntegrityViolationException` because they cannot inspect a driver error label, that retrying a genuine
integrity violation is wasteful rather than wrong, and that the Spring executors treat a duplicate key as retryable. The Decision below corrects all three for the executors. The stores keep
retrying a duplicate key of their own. Resolves [#1379](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1379).

## Context

ADR 21 lists, among its positive consequences, "Contention surfaces as a retry, not a spurious command failure." That
holds only until the retry runs out. `SpringMongoEventStore` and `ReactorMongoEventStore` retried a DCB append that
lost a transaction conflict 15 times, which is about 4.6 seconds of waiting with the backoff capped at 500 ms. When
many appends write the same marker document, the last of them can lose to every other one, and then the 15th failure
reached the caller as the command's failure. #1379 measured that on a loaded single-node MongoDB 8.0: 69 of 1038
commands failed with 64 threads on one type marker. Each failure took about 5 seconds.

The native `MongoEventStore` did not fail in the same test. It runs the append through the driver's
`ClientSession.withTransaction`, which keeps retrying a transient transaction error for up to 120 seconds a call. The Spring
stores run the transaction through Spring's transaction manager, which retries nothing, so their own attempts were the
whole budget.

## Decision

Both Spring stores retry a transient transaction conflict for about two minutes of waiting, the 120 seconds that one
`withTransaction` call gives the native store. The retry stops after a number of attempts, so the time each attempt
takes comes on top of the waiting, and also once 120 seconds have passed since the first attempt began, which is after the position block was reserved. The deadline is there
because the driver labels a failure to select a server in an active transaction as transient too. With no primary an
attempt can take about 30 seconds, and 240 of them would be two hours.

- `SpringMongoEventStore` makes 240 attempts in total with the backoff it already had, 10 ms doubling up to 500 ms.
- `ReactorMongoEventStore` makes 320 retries, which is 321 attempts in all, with the same backoff. Reactor's default
  jitter makes each wait between 250 and 500 ms once the backoff reaches its cap, 375 ms on average, so 320 retries
  add up to about as much waiting as 240 attempts do on the blocking store.
- The default `SpringTransactionExecutor` and `SpringReactiveTransactionExecutor` get the same budget and the same
  deadline, and they retry on the error label and not on `DataIntegrityViolationException`. See the next paragraph. With synchronous subscriptions and the default propagation the executor owns the transaction, the store joins it and
  retries nothing, so the executor's retry is the whole budget there. An executor built on a template or operator
  that opens no transaction means the store retries as well. A retry passed to an executor's constructor is used as given.
- `ReactorMongoEventStore` retries a lost `any()` version race 320 times too. See Consequences.
- The default executors retry a `TransientDataAccessException`, or any exception that has the `TransientTransactionError`
  label anywhere in its cause chain. The label is what MongoDB puts on an error that a new transaction can get past,
  and it is what the driver's own `withTransaction` retries on. ADR 74 matched `DataIntegrityViolationException` instead,
  because Spring translates a WriteConflict to it and the executor modules did not look at the driver. That also matched a
  duplicate key and a validation failure, which have no label. The two executor modules now depend on
  `mongodb-driver-core` as an optional dependency and look for the label only when `com.mongodb.MongoException` is on the
  classpath, so an application without the driver still gets the executor and still retries a `TransientDataAccessException`.
  A commit that fails with the `UnknownTransactionCommitResult` label is not retried even though a commit failure
  can have both labels, since the commit may have gone through and running the unit of work again could apply it twice.
- A commit that fails with the transient label is retried at most twice, three runs in all. That label on a commit
  covers three causes that the error cannot tell apart. They are a failover, a transaction that outlived
  `transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds`, and a write error that the unit of work caught and swallowed, because MongoDB
  aborts the transaction on that error. Each gives `NoSuchTransaction` (code 251) with the transient label. I ran all
  three against a three-member MongoDB 8.0 replica set with the blocking and the reactive executor. A failover and an
  expiry succeed on the second run. A swallowed error fails on every run, and without a cap it ran 217 times in 120
  seconds. Three runs survive two failovers in a row and not three, and every run added to the cap is another rerun of the
  swallowed case. The count belongs to one call and counts failed commits only, so an error thrown from the unit of work, a
  transaction exception included, keeps the full budget. At the cap the executor throws a `TransactionSystemException` that names the error and the
  count, and for code 251 it lists the three causes without choosing one. An executor built with a retry of its own has
  no cap.
- Not retrying a failed commit at all, or not retrying code 251, was considered and rejected, since both give up the
  failover and the expiry that this retry is for. The failover message differs from the other two, but an expiry and a
  swallowed error have the same code, labels and message, and a message is not something to match on.
- There is no setting for the count or the deadline and no extra jitter. A user who needs another budget can raise it
  when a need shows up.
- The retry still runs only when the store owns the transaction, as in [ADR 74](0074-retry-only-where-the-transaction-is-owned.md).

Moving the stores to `ClientSession.withTransaction` was considered and rejected. It would bypass the
`TransactionTemplate` the user configured, and the reactive driver has no such method.

## Consequences

- ADR 21's sentence is true with a limit. An append that contends on a marker document gets up to 240 attempts on the
  blocking store and 321 on the reactive one, which is about two minutes of waiting. A caller that loses every
  attempt still gets the last failure. In the case #1379 measured that was a `DataIntegrityViolationException`, and
  `GenericDcbApplicationService` does not retry that exception.
- A command that used to fail after about 5 seconds under heavy contention now waits about two minutes in all, across
  attempts that each wait 10 to 500 ms, before it fails, plus the time the attempts themselves take. A command that
  `GenericDcbApplicationService` runs again after a failed append condition can spend that time on each of its runs. No retry is scheduled once 120 seconds have
  passed since the first attempt began, but one scheduled just before then still starts after its backoff of up to
  500 ms, and an attempt that is already running is not interrupted and ends on the driver's own timeouts, as it does
  in a native `withTransaction` call. The native store's 120 seconds applies to each `withTransaction` call, and its append runs that
  call inside a retry of 15 attempts, so the native store can wait longer overall. A caller with a shorter deadline of
  its own sees that deadline first.
- A duplicate key or a validation failure inside the transaction now runs the unit of work once and reaches the caller,
  as against the 214 runs in 120 seconds that a duplicate key got in a measurement of the old predicate under the new budget on MongoDB 8.0. 0.34.0 itself ran it 15 times on the blocking executor and 16 on the reactive one.
  One case that was retried before is not any more. It is a duplicate from a write made outside the transaction, for
  example through a template that does not join it. MongoDB labels no such error, so a unit of work that checks, loses
  a race to a rival and then gets the duplicate used to succeed on its second run, and now fails with the duplicate. A
  caller that relied on it handles the duplicate itself, or does the write through a template that joins the transaction.
- A commit that fails with `UnknownTransactionCommitResult` is never retried, also when the same error has the
  `TransientTransactionError` label. The old predicate did not retry it either, since a commit failure surfaces as a
  `TransactionSystemException` with a `MongoException` cause, which it did not match. The same reason means a commit
  that fails with only the transient label, which the old predicate did not retry, is retried now. That includes a unit of work that catches a duplicate key from a write inside the transaction and returns normally. The server has aborted the transaction and the commit fails with the transient label, so the unit of work runs three times and then fails with a message that names the commit, where 0.34.0 failed once. The executor cannot tell that commit from a failover, so the caller has to let such a duplicate propagate.
- The budget of 240 attempts and 120 seconds was chosen when a retry could be spent on an error no retry could cure. Now
  that only a conflict uses it, I measured how much a conflict needs, on a single-node MongoDB 8.0 with a
  `TransientTransactionError` predicate. 64 threads appending 10 times each to one marker needed at most 21 attempts, and 256
  threads appending 3 times each needed at most 36, in runs that took 46 seconds. None of the 768 commands in the larger run
  failed. The budget is about seven times the worst case seen, so it stays. The measurement does not cover a stuck rival
  transaction, which can hold a document for up to a minute under the server's default transaction lifetime, and the 120
  second budget is what rides that out.
- A reserved position block is still abandoned when an append exhausts its retries, so `dcbposition` can still have
  gaps, as ADR 21 says.
- The reactive stream write retries a lost version race for an append with `StreamVersionWriteCondition.any()`. That is a
  different condition from the one above, and it had the same 15-retry limit. 64 writers appending 20 unconditional
  events each to one stream lost 7 of 1280 writes to it on a single-node MongoDB 8.0, where the blocking stores retry
  with no limit at all. It now makes 320 retries too, which lost none in the same test. [ADR 80](0080-concurrent-write-conformance.md)
  describes the 15, and is corrected here. This retry has no deadline of its own, and the blocking stores' retry of the
  same race has no limit at all.

adrs.title: A DCB consistency token belongs to the criteria it was read with
adrs.author: Johan Haleby
adrs.status_raw: Accepted. Decides [#1228](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1228) and the first part of [#1229](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1229). Amends [ADR 21](0021-dcb-write-path-query-scoped-concurrency.md), [ADR 30](0030-keep-matchall-dcb-append-condition-with-documented-limi
adrs.text:
# 147. A DCB consistency token belongs to the criteria it was read with

Date: 2026-10-23

## Status

Accepted. Decides [#1228](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1228) and the first part of
[#1229](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1229). Amends
[ADR 21](0021-dcb-write-path-query-scoped-concurrency.md),
[ADR 30](0030-keep-matchall-dcb-append-condition-with-documented-limit.md),
[ADR 31](0031-capture-dcb-consistency-token-in-a-single-read.md), [ADR 53](0053-dcb-api-freeze-consistency.md) and
[ADR 88](0088-what-a-dcb-append-condition-guarantees.md).

The second part of #1229 and [#1231](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1231) are not decided here.
[ADR 162](0162-a-dcb-type-marker-is-split-into-stripes.md) decides the first and
[ADR 149](0149-the-mongodb-dcb-append-check-compares-each-marker-and-then-the-events-above-it.md) the second.

## Context

A command on a DCB consistency boundary reads the events matching some criteria and gets a `DcbConsistencyToken` back
on the `DcbEventStream`. It then appends with a `DcbAppendCondition` that holds criteria and that token, and the store
is meant to refuse the append with `DcbAppendConditionNotFulfilledException` when an event matching the condition's
criteria was committed after the read.

In 0.34 the token is `record DcbConsistencyToken(long value)`. The in-memory store puts its read head in it and looks
for a matching event above that position. The three MongoDB stores put the sum of the versions of the read criteria's
marker documents in it (ADR 21, ADR 31), and the append compares that sum with the sum over the condition's criteria.
That design has two problems.

**The token doesn't know which criteria it was read with** (#1228). Nothing stops a condition from using other criteria
than the read, and on MongoDB the check then compares sums over different markers. Say a command reads `tags(a)` while
`tag:a` is at 3, so the token is 3, and then appends with `tags(b)`. Another command appends an event tagged `b` in
between and takes `tag:b` from 2 to 3. The check reads 3 for `tag:b`, finds it equal to the token, and lets the append
through although an event matching its criteria was committed after the read. The in-memory store compares positions
instead, so the same code is refused there.

**A type in the criteria makes the boundary store-wide** (#1229). `DcbMarkerModel.queryMarkerKeys` gives every
criteria item a `tag:` key for each of its tags and a `type:` key for each of its types, and every append increments
`type:X` for each type it writes. A command that reads `type("InvoiceIssued").tags(invoice1)` therefore conflicts with
an append of an `InvoiceIssued` tagged `invoice2`, which doesn't match it. The two appends also increment the same
`type:InvoiceIssued` document, so MongoDB doesn't let them commit at the same time. ADR 21 accepted false conflicts
between appends that share a tag or a type, as the boundary the caller chose. For an item with tags, though, the type
is shared with every event of that type in the store, and the boundary the caller chose is the tag.

## Decision

### The token holds the criteria it was read with

`DcbConsistencyToken` becomes a final class with two private fields, the criteria the read used and a version whose
meaning the store defines. The version is the read head in memory and the marker sum on MongoDB. A store creates a
token with `DcbConsistencyToken.of(DcbCriteria, long)`, and `criteria()` returns the read criteria. `version()` is
there for store implementations, the way `value()` is in 0.34, and nothing outside a store should read or keep it. Two
tokens are equal when their criteria are the same, as defined in the next section, and their versions are equal.

These are removed:

- The public constructor, `DcbConsistencyToken.of(long)` and `value()`.
- `DcbEventStream(List, long)` and `DcbDomainEventStream(List, long)`, because they create a token with no criteria.

The token is a class and not a record so that a field can be added later as a new factory overload, which a record's
public canonical constructor and accessors don't allow without breaking. A read position, which #1231 may need, would
be such a field. It isn't added now, since what it should mean depends on the same decision about reserving positions.

### When two criteria are the same

Two criteria are the same when they hold the same set of alternatives:

- `DcbCriteria.all()` is the same only as `DcbCriteria.all()`.
- A `DcbCriterion` is the same as an `anyOf(..)` holding only that criterion.
- Two `anyOf(..)` are the same when they hold the same criteria in any order, so `anyOf(a, b)` is the same as
  `anyOf(b, a)`.

Criteria that select the same events but are built differently aren't the same. `types("A", "B")` and
`anyOf(type("A"), type("B"))` are an example. `DcbCriteria.equals` doesn't change, and it still compares an `anyOf(..)`
in order. `DcbSnapshotKeys.canonicalKey` doesn't change either, so no stored snapshot key moves.

### A condition refuses a token with other criteria

`DcbAppendCondition`'s constructor throws `IllegalArgumentException` when the token's criteria aren't the same as the
condition's criteria. Every factory goes through the constructor, so the refusal happens before any store is called.
No store reserves positions or writes markers for it, and a `DcbEventStore` of your own gets the check without doing
anything. With its default retry, `defaultRetryStrategy()` on the blocking stack and `defaultRetry()` on the reactor
stack, `GenericDcbApplicationService` retries only `DcbAppendConditionNotFulfilledException`, so the
`IllegalArgumentException` reaches the caller on the first attempt.

- `DcbAppendCondition.failIfEventsMatch(DcbConsistencyToken)` is added and takes its criteria from the token. Both
  `GenericDcbApplicationService` classes and the `InvoiceService` example switch to it.
- `failIfEventsMatch(DcbCriteria, DcbConsistencyToken)` is deprecated, and its javadoc points at the one-argument
  form. It keeps working and refuses a token with other criteria the same way.
- `wholeStoreLock(DcbConsistencyToken)` stays, since its name says the condition covers the whole store. It refuses a
  token whose criteria aren't `DcbCriteria.all()`.

The rule is the same on every store. Code that reads with one criteria and appends with another, passing the token
the read returned, throws on the in-memory store as it does on MongoDB, so a test against the in-memory store can catch
it before production.

### Query markers for an item with tags

`DcbMarkerModel.queryMarkerKeys` gives an item that has at least one tag only its `tag:` keys. An item without tags gets
its `type:` keys as before, and `DcbCriteria.all()` keeps the `all` key. `eventMarkerKeys` doesn't change, so every
append still increments a marker for each tag and each type of its events.

ADR 21's argument for the marker check still holds for an item with tags. An event matches the item only when it has all
of the item's tags, so an append of a matching event increments every one of the item's `tag:` markers, and a token over
those markers moves with it. A conditional append on the item increments the same markers from its query keys, so the
two appends share a document and MongoDB doesn't let them commit at the same time. An item without tags keeps its type
keys, and excluded types never had keys.

Sharing a type with a criteria item that has tags is no longer a reason for the check to refuse. Two appends of the same
type that run at the same time still conflict, whatever their tags. Every append still increments `type:X`, so both
write the same marker document and MongoDB doesn't let them commit at the same time. That is the second part of #1229.

### Invariants

- **I1.** For a condition with criteria `Ca` and a token whose criteria are `Ct`, the condition can't be created when
  `Ca` isn't the same as `Ct`. It throws `IllegalArgumentException` and no store is called.
- **I2.** For an item `i` with tags and an event `e` matching `i`, the markers an append of `e` increments include
  every query marker of `i`. For an item `i` without tags, they include at least one query marker of `i`.

Apart from I1 and the query markers in I2, what a store refuses for a condition is what ADR 21 and ADR 88 decided.

I1 compares criteria and nothing else. A token used on another store instance, built with `of` outside a store, or
saved and turned back into a token later gets past it whenever its criteria match the condition's. `of` is public
because the stores live in other modules than the token, and a `DcbEventStore` of your own needs it too.

### Upgrading

This change adds nothing on disk. The marker documents and their ids stay the same, so it doesn't stop 0.34 and 0.35
nodes appending to the same store. An item with tags no longer adds its type markers to what a conditional append from
a 0.35 node increments. A conditional append from a 0.34 node also increments type markers. 0.35 doesn't read those for
criteria with tags, so they make no such check refuse, and an increment only ever raises a version, so it can't make a
check let an append through. This change doesn't stop you going back to 0.34
either. The upgrade guide says what else in 0.35 limits a rolling upgrade or a rollback.

A token value saved under 0.34 isn't valid on 0.35. For a criteria item with both types and tags it is a sum over tag
and type markers, while 0.35 no longer counts that item's type markers, so an old value can let an append through that should have been
refused. The migration guide tells anyone who saved a token value, in an ETag or a queued command for example, to read
again instead. Occurrent itself doesn't save a token.

## Alternatives considered

**Allow narrower criteria where the store can check them** (option 2 in #1228). The same code would then pass in memory
and throw on MongoDB.

**Allow an item with tags to keep only some of its types, or to exclude more types.** Once query markers for an item
with tags are its tags only, such a condition has the same markers as the read, so every store could check it. It
would write the marker model's structure into the public API, though, and it removes no conflict on MongoDB. Allowing
it later turns a refusal into an acceptance, which doesn't break anyone, while allowing it now and refusing it later
would.

**Fit the criteria into the `long`, as a hash or as bits.** A hash collision can let an append through, which is the
defect this ADR fixes. Bits for the criteria leave no room in 64 bits for anything else the token may need.

**Add the read position to the token now.** What it should mean depends on how positions get reserved, and it would
repeat `DcbEventStream.lastSequencePosition()` until then.

**Give the token a string form** for sending it to a client and back. Nothing in the repository needs one, and a stable
encoding is a wire format to keep compatible. The final class lets it be added later.

**Let only the store instance that read a token accept it.** Each store would get its own token type, with an id for
the store instance, and check that a condition holds one of its own. That would cover a token used on another store
instance. A `DcbEventStore` of your own still needs a public way to create a token, though, so a caller can still build
one by hand. Every store implementation would need the token type and the check, and the TCK would need tests for it.
#1228 is about code that reads with one criteria and appends with another by mistake, and the criteria in the token
catch that.

## Consequences

- A condition built from a read's token and other criteria than the read's throws, on every store.
- On the MongoDB stores, sharing a type with a criteria item that has tags is no longer a reason for the check to
  refuse. The in-memory store doesn't refuse for that either, so the TCK asserts the same answer on every store for an
  unconditional append that only shares a type. A

adrs.title: Capture the DCB consistency token in a single consistent read
adrs.author: Johan Haleby
adrs.status_raw: Accepted Amended by [ADR 147](0147-a-dcb-consistency-token-belongs-to-the-criteria-it-was-read-with.md). The token is no longer a `long`. adrs.text:
# 31. Capture the DCB consistency token in a single consistent read

Date: 2026-06-28

## Status

Accepted

Amended by [ADR 147](0147-a-dcb-consistency-token-belongs-to-the-criteria-it-was-read-with.md). The token is no longer a `long`. It holds the criteria it was read with and a version
the store defines. Reading all of a query's markers in a single read still stands.

Amended by [ADR 149](0149-the-mongodb-dcb-append-check-compares-each-marker-and-then-the-events-above-it.md). A find can yield between documents, and through a mongos it reads each shard on its own, so a single read of the markers isn't one point in time.

## Context

ADR 0021 defines the DCB consistency token as the sum of the versions of a query's conflict markers, captured when the query is read and rechecked inside the append transaction. The append recheck reads the markers inside its transaction, so it sees one consistent snapshot. The read-time capture did not: it read each marker with a separate `findById`, outside any session or transaction.

For a query with more than one marker, for example `tagsAllOf("t1","t2")` whose markers are `tag:t1` and `tag:t2`, an append committing between the per-marker reads produces a token that belongs to no single point in time. Because the token is a scalar sum, a torn capture can equal a later genuine sum and let the append recheck pass when it should fail, which is a missed conflict and so a write skew. The scalar sum is sound only when the markers are read as one consistent snapshot, because then any matching append strictly increases the sum.

## Decision

Capture the token by reading all of a query's markers in a single read, so the per-marker versions come from one point in time. The token stays a `long`, since a sum over a consistent snapshot is a sound "did any of my markers move" check and needs no per-marker version map.

## Consequences

- The multi-marker write-skew window is closed. A single matching append now always moves the captured sum.
- The token representation is unchanged, so `DcbConsistencyToken` and the in-transaction recheck are untouched.
- A regression test drives a multi-marker query with an interleaved scoped append, which the previous per-marker capture could not catch.

adrs.author: Johan Haleby

adrs.text:
# 74. Retry a write conflict only where the transaction is owned

Date: 2026-07-26

## Status

Accepted. Amended by [ADR 149](0149-the-mongodb-dcb-append-check-compares-each-marker-and-then-the-events-above-it.md)
on what an append in a caller's transaction conflicts on, which exception the blocking store throws for a write
conflict, how the Spring stores tell a caller's transaction, and that the counter update retries inside one.

## Context

The DCB write path retries a conflict between concurrent appends. In the Spring Mongo stores that retry wrapped the whole transaction:

```java
return executeWithTransientRetry(() -> transactionTemplate.execute(...));
```

`TransactionTemplate` uses `PROPAGATION_REQUIRED`, and the store sets `SessionSynchronization.ALWAYS`, so when a transaction is already open the template joins it rather than starting one of its own. The retry then cannot work. The first attempt hits a write conflict, MongoDB aborts the transaction, and every later attempt rejoins that dead transaction and fails on its first read with error 251 `NoSuchTransaction`. That error carries the `TransientTransactionError` label, so the retry predicate keeps matching and all 15 attempts are spent, about 5 seconds, before the failure propagates anyway.

Two situations put a transaction around the append. An application can wrap a command in `@Transactional`. Occurrent itself does it whenever a synchronous subscription is registered, because `GenericDcbApplicationService` runs the whole read-decide-append through a `TransactionExecutor` so the write and the handlers commit together.

The native driver store never had the problem. It looks for an ambient `ClientSession` and, when it finds one, runs the append body once without opening a session, starting a transaction, or retrying. The two Spring stores were simply missing the equivalent check, so this is a gap between the four DCB stores rather than a new policy.

## Decision

A retry never spans a transaction its layer does not own, because only the code that began a transaction can begin a fresh one. Each layer therefore either owns the transaction and retries, or participates in someone else's and runs once.

The two Spring Mongo stores check for an active transaction before choosing. `SpringMongoEventStore` uses `TransactionSynchronizationManager.isActualTransactionActive()`, and `ReactorMongoEventStore` uses `ReactiveMongoDatabaseUtils.isTransactionActive(...)` to read the reactive context. When a transaction is already active they run the append body once and let the conflict reach whoever owns it.

The retry that the store gives up is picked up by the layer that does own the transaction. `SpringTransactionExecutor` and `SpringReactiveTransactionExecutor` retry a conflict around the transaction they open, and skip the retry when they are themselves joining a caller's transaction. That keeps the synchronous-subscription configuration retrying, one level up, where each attempt genuinely starts a fresh transaction.

When neither the store nor the executor owns the transaction, nothing in the library retries and the conflict reaches the application immediately. That is the intended outcome. The application has to retry at its own transaction boundary. The word-guessing-game example shows the shape: its use cases dropped a `@Transactional` that was doing nothing but disabling the store's retry, and added the transient type to their `@Retryable`, which works because retry advice sits outside transaction advice so each attempt gets a fresh transaction.

The rule is enforced through a single `retryOnlyWhenThisStoreOwnsTheTransaction` helper in each Spring store, and every retry on the write path goes through it: the DCB append, the position counter's cold start, and the stream `write` condition retry. Routing them through one place is deliberate. The counter retry was written without an ownership check, and it is exactly the kind of site that gets added again later.

That includes the stream `write` path even though this decision was driven by DCB. Its any-version retry has the same weakness, and worse consequences: joined to a caller's transaction, a thrown `WriteConditionNotFulfilledException` marks that transaction rollback-only, so a further attempt participates in a transaction whose inner commit is a no-op and `write` can report a success the caller cannot keep. Leaving one retry outside the rule would also have made the helper's own contract false.

The two Spring stacks change together, so the retry parity recorded in [ADR 53](0053-dcb-api-freeze-consistency.md) still holds between them. The in-memory store needs none of this because it has no transactions. The native driver is consistent in shape but not in policy, and that is accepted rather than corrected here: `NativeMongoTransactionExecutor` runs its work through `ClientSession.withTransaction`, so the driver itself re-runs the body on a `TransientTransactionError` until its own deadline rather than for a bounded number of attempts, and it does not treat a duplicate key as retryable the way the Spring stores and executors do.

## Consequences

Retrying at the caller's own transaction boundary is not merely the recommended remedy, it is the only one that works. A participating `TransactionTemplate.execute` that throws marks the surrounding transaction rollback-only, so an application that catches the conflict and carries on inside the same transaction gets `UnexpectedRollbackException` at commit instead of the partial success it expected.

The executors match `DataIntegrityViolationException` as well as `TransientDataAccessException`. These are Spring's translated types, used because the executor modules are storage-neutral and cannot inspect a driver error label the way the stores do. MongoDB's WriteConflict makes this necessary rather than merely convenient: the server labels it `TransientTransactionError`, yet Spring translates it to `DataIntegrityViolationException`, which is a non-transient type, so a predicate built only on `TransientDataAccessException` would miss the most common conflict there is. The cost is that a genuine integrity violation, say a synchronous subscription handler hitting a unique index, is retried too. That is wasteful rather than wrong, since it fails the same way every attempt and then propagates.

Position reservation behaves differently depending on ownership, and the comments in both stores now say so. [ADR 21](0021-dcb-write-path-query-scoped-concurrency.md) describes the counter `findAndModify` as running outside the append transaction, which holds only while the store owns that transaction. When the store joins a caller's transaction the counter update joins it too, so one shared document becomes a conflict point for every concurrent append in that transaction, even for appends to disjoint boundaries. In practice a nested append often loses on the counter before it ever reaches the append body, which is worth knowing when reading a failure. A test measuring this saw only one of six contended appends reach the body at all.

The retry the executors apply covers the whole unit of work, which for a synchronous-subscription setup includes the handlers. A handler with a side effect outside the transaction, an HTTP call say, can therefore run more than once for one command. That was already true of the application service's existing append-condition retry, so it is not a new class of behaviour, but it now has a second trigger. The two retries do not compound, because their predicates are disjoint: the executor matches only data-access conflicts and the service only `DcbAppendConditionNotFulfilledException`.

A conflict inside a caller-owned transaction now fails immediately instead of after roughly 5 seconds of attempts that could never have committed, so the failure is both faster and easier to attribute.

adrs.text:
# 88. What a DCB append condition guarantees, and the one thing it does not

Date: 2026-08-02

## Status

Accepted. Part of #394, TCK phase 4.

Amended by [ADR 147](0147-a-dcb-consistency-token-belongs-to-the-criteria-it-was-read-with.md). A condition can't be created with a token that holds other criteria than its own, and throws
`IllegalArgumentException` before any store is called. On the MongoDB stores, sharing a type with a criteria item that
has tags is no longer a reason for the check to refuse, as in memory.

Amended by [ADR 149](0149-the-mongodb-dcb-append-check-compares-each-marker-and-then-the-events-above-it.md). On a replica set the MongoDB stores no longer refuse an append for an event a 0.35 node appended that shares a tag
with the criteria and doesn't match them, so the answer for an excluded type is the same as in memory there. On a
sharded cluster the store still refuses when a marker of the criteria moved. On a replica set it can still refuse when 0.34 wrote the marker, which ADR 149 describes.

## Context

DCB is the biggest block of untested-in-common behaviour left in #394: roughly 5,300 lines of DCB test code across the
four stores, with the largest test files in the repository sitting in it. Deduplicating that is worth doing on its own,
but DCB is also the first phase where the stores disagree about *behaviour* rather than about representation, so the
question the TCK has to answer first is which disagreements are contract and which are variation.

Two of them are real, and they are not independent. Occurrent has two ways of answering a token-qualified
`DcbAppendCondition`:

- The in-memory store compares the events committed after the token against the condition's criteria, exactly as a read
  would.
- The three MongoDB stores compare version markers kept per consistency boundary, so the check is a single conditional
  write rather than a scan (ADR 21).

The marker model is coarser, and coarseness cuts both ways:

| Scenario | Exact criteria | Tag markers |
|---|---|---|
| An excluded type sharing a boundary tag, committed after the read | no conflict | conflicts |
| `wholeStoreLock(token)` against a later tag-scoped append | conflicts | no conflict |

The first is a false conflict, sound and self-healing: the application service re-reads the still-excluded boundary and
retries. The second is a false pass, which is the limitation `wholeStoreLock()` already documents in as many words and
the reason it is correct only for a single writer or an empty-store guard (ADR 30).

A third divergence looked like a candidate and is not one. In-memory advances its position counter only on commit, so a
rejected append consumes no position, while the MongoDB stores reserve a block outside the write transaction and
abandon it, leaving a permanent gap. Three per-store tests pin their own answer to that.

## Decision

**One fixture declaration, `appendConditionModel()`, returning `EXACT_CRITERIA` or `TAG_MARKER`.** The suite asserts
the documented outcome for whichever is declared, and both branches run in this repository, so neither is a claim
nobody checks.

One declaration rather than one per symptom, because the two symptoms are one fact seen from either side. A model that
is coarse over-approximates for a criteria narrower than its boundary and under-approximates for a boundary wider than
the markers a scoped append touches. The two constants therefore give opposite answers to both rows of the table above,
which is why one answer settles them both. It is an enum rather than a boolean because both models deserve a name, and
it has no default because there is no answer that is right often enough to inherit: getting it wrong makes the suite
assert the opposite of what the store does.

**It is a declaration rather than a question put to the store**, which is the side of ADR 84's line that
`timePrecision()` sits on. The model is a property of how the write path is built and no method on `DcbEventStore`
reports it, so there is nothing to ask. The rule stands unchanged: declare what cannot be asked, ask everything else.

**The position-gap divergence gets no declaration at all.** ADR 84 already settled that a position is positive, unique
and strictly increasing, and explicitly not dense. A gap after a rejected append is that contract being honoured, not
a variation on it, so the suite asserts neither outcome and asserts contiguity only *within* one append, which is what
`DcbAppendResult` actually promises. A fixture flag here would have recorded two stores' implementation details as if
they were behaviour.

**The reactive bridge learns DCB.** `BlockingEventStoreOverReactive` already presents the reactive stream API as a
blocking one so the behavioural suites are written once; it now presents the reactive `DcbEventStore` the same way. The
two APIs mirror each other method for method and share every value type, so the delegation is one to one.

This is not tidiness. The reactor store shares the marker model with the two MongoDB stores that are thoroughly
tested, and is itself the least tested of the four: no type-versus-tag skew case, no multi-marker boundary, no
tokenless guard, and same-boundary contention at 3 iterations against the other two stores' 50. Running it through the
shared suite closes that in one move rather than by hand-writing the missing tests a second time.

**A second suite, `DcbStreamInteropConformance`, requires STREAM and DCB together.** Six assertions need both
capabilities: that a DCB read never returns a stream-written event and vice versa, that a stream write refuses an event
carrying DCB tags, that one global position sequence covers both modes, and that a condition with no token means
"currently exists" rather than "ever appended", which can only be shown by deleting the match. Requiring the pair in
its own suite keeps `DcbEventStoreConformance` runnable by a DCB-only store, and keeps a store's reason for not running
these a visible missing subclass rather than a skip.

## Consequences

A store's fixture now answers one more question, and answering it wrong is a loud failure rather than a silent one: the
suite asserts the other model's outcome and the assertion message names which model it expected. A store that changes
its write path has to change the declaration in the same commit.

The list of things the suite deliberately does not assert is longer here than in any earlier phase, and it is written
into the suite's own javadoc rather than only here, because several of the omissions are tempting:

- **A consistency token's value.** Opaque and store-internal, so it is round-tripped and never read. Two tokens from
  the same store are compared for equality where the contract promises they are equal, which is a different thing from
  interpreting one.
- **`lastSequencePosition` as a concurrency boundary.** It is the store's DCB head, not the highest matched position,
  and it reports the head even for a read that matched nothing. A store assigning positions before its events commit
  can report a head ahead of what a reader can see, which is why the token type exists at all.
- **Which storage stream a DCB event landed in.** Placement is derived from tags and `DcbStreamIdGenerator`'s own
  javadoc calls it a storage placement choice, not part of the DCB contract.
- **How `exists` and `count` are implemented.** Both document a full read as their default and invite an implementation
  to do better, so asserting call counts or efficiency would pin the default rather than the contract.

Left per store on purpose, unchanged from earlier phases: Mongo index and explain-plan assertions, transaction
ownership (ADR 74), driver exception translation, the read-watermark and unconditional-marker regression tests, which
are regressions against the marker implementation rather than against the contract, and the capability-gating tests
that belong to phase 5.

One thing the suite does assert verbatim that a reader might expect it to loosen: the message on
`DcbAppendConditionNotFulfilledException`, and the message a stream write produces when handed a DCB-tagged event. Both
are fixed literals with nothing interpolated, and both are built independently in four places while coming out
identical, so a store drifting away from either is worth a failing test. That is the same call made for
`WriteConditionNotFulfilledException` and the opposite of the one made for `DuplicateCloudEventException`, whose
message carries raw driver text on the MongoDB stores and nothing in memory.

adrs.title: The MongoDB DCB append check compares each marker, and then the events above it
adrs.author: Johan Haleby

Amends [ADR 21](0021-dcb-write-path-query-scoped-concurrency.md) on how the append check compares a token and on pruning markers, [ADR 88](0088-what-a-dc
adrs.text:
# 149. The MongoDB DCB append check compares each marker, and then the events above it

Date: 2026-10-30

## Status

Accepted. Decides [#1231](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1231) and
[#1300](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1300). Amends
[ADR 21](0021-dcb-write-path-query-scoped-concurrency.md) on how the append check compares a token and on pruning
markers, [ADR 88](0088-what-a-dcb-append-condition-guarantees.md) on what the MongoDB stores answer for an excluded
type, [ADR 147](0147-a-dcb-consistency-token-belongs-to-the-criteria-it-was-read-with.md) on what the token holds, and
[ADR 31](0031-capture-dcb-consistency-token-in-a-single-read.md) on what one read of the markers gives, and
[ADR 74](0074-retry-only-where-the-transaction-is-owned.md) on an append in a caller's transaction.
Builds on the marker versions of [ADR 148](0148-dcb-snapshots-resume-from-marker-versions-not-positions.md).

The second part of [#1229](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1229), splitting each type marker into
several documents, is decided in [ADR 162](0162-a-dcb-type-marker-is-split-into-stripes.md). The check below works
on whatever marker keys a criteria has, so it holds for those documents too.

## Context

A conditional DCB append on the three MongoDB stores compares one number. The read sums the versions of the marker
documents of its criteria into the token, and the append sums them again inside its transaction and refuses when the
two sums differ (`MongoEventStore.java:708`, `SpringMongoEventStore.java:829`, `ReactorMongoEventStore.java:584`). That
sum has two problems.

**It moves for appends that don't match the criteria** (#1231). After ADR 147, the markers of an item with tags are
its `tag:` markers, and every append increments a marker for every tag of its events. So the check refuses in three
cases where no matching event was committed after the read:

- **Another type with the same tag.** The criteria is `type("TicketSold").tags(concert:k1)`, and a `ConcertRenamed`
  tagged `concert:k1` is committed after the read.
- **Only some of the item's tags.** The criteria is `type("StudentEnrolledInCourse").tags(course:c1, student:s1)`,
  and an enrolment of `s2` in `c1` is committed after the read.
- **An excluded type with the same tag.** The criteria excludes `CourseRenamed`, and a `CourseRenamed` tagged
  `course:c1` is committed after the read.

The in-memory store doesn't refuse in any of them, because it compares the events committed after the token with the
criteria. The issue's own idea, an exact query for matching events above the read position, isn't sound on MongoDB. A
store reserves positions before the append transaction starts (`MongoEventStore.java:642`), so an event can commit
below a position a reader has already seen. ADR 148 keeps that, and reserving inside the transaction would make every
append in the store conflict with every other one (ADR 148, design 3).

**It doesn't notice that a marker was pruned** (#1300). ADR 21 lets an operator delete marker documents during
quiescence and calls that harmless, and so do the comments above `incrementConflictMarkers` in the native and Spring
stores. A token can be held much longer than a quiet moment, for example by a command waiting in a queue. Say a command reads
`tags(a)` while `tag:a` is at version 1. The marker is deleted, another command appends an event tagged `a`, and the
upsert creates `tag:a` again at version 1. The first command then appends with its token, and the sums are equal. A
prune can also lower one marker while another goes up, so two different states of the markers can give the same sum.

Since ADR 148, a 0.35 store keeps three things that change this. Every marker document has an `epoch`, which is new
each time the marker is created. Every marker has a counter `s` of the increments that wrote marker versions on their
events, so `version - s` (called u below) counts the increments of a writer that wrote none. And every event a 0.35
writer appends has an `mv` array, with the key, the epoch and the version its transaction gave each of its markers.
ADR 148 also showed that, per key, marker versions follow commit order. Two transactions can't both increment one
marker, because MongoDB aborts one of them with a write conflict, and the one that retries reads the other's commit.

## Decision

### The token holds what the read saw of each marker

`DcbConsistencyToken` gets a third field. It holds, for each marker key of the read's criteria, the marker's epoch,
its version and its u, as the read saw them. A marker the read didn't find is recorded with no epoch, version 0 and u 0.

- `DcbConsistencyToken.of(DcbCriteria, long, Map<String, DcbConsistencyToken.MarkerObservation>)` is added, with
  `record MarkerObservation(@Nullable String epoch, long version, long unstamped)`.
- `markers()` returns the map, which is empty for a token made with `of(DcbCriteria, long)`.
- Two tokens are equal when their criteria are the same, their versions are equal and their maps are equal.

Like `version()`, the map is for store implementations. ADR 147 made the token a final class so that a field could
be added this way. A `DcbEventStore` of your own can keep using `of(DcbCriteria, long)`, and a MongoDB store refuses a
token made that way, as the next section says. The MongoDB stores keep the sum in `version()`.
`MarkerObservation` replaces the stores' internal `ObservedMarker`. It can't be `DcbMarkerVersions.MarkerVersion`,
which requires an epoch and a version of at least 1, because a token also has to hold a marker that was missing or
had no epoch.

Every MongoDB read already loads the marker documents to sum them (`MongoEventStore.java:764-782`), and the marker
documents already hold the epoch and `s`. So the map costs no extra read. Each store fills it on every read path,
the one that asks for versions, the one that doesn't and the catch-up read scope.

### The check compares each marker

Inside the append transaction, the store reads the condition's markers as it does today and compares each one with
the token's map, never the sums. A token whose map doesn't hold exactly the condition's marker keys wasn't read
by this store, and the append throws `IllegalArgumentException`. That includes the empty map of a token made with
`of(DcbCriteria, long)`.

1. When a marker the token saw has another epoch, or is gone, or has a lower version, the check refuses. That's a
   prune or a recreated marker, and it's #1300's fix. A marker the read didn't find isn't one the token saw, so that
   marker existing now is no reason to refuse.
2. When every marker has the token's version, the check passes, as it does today.
3. Otherwise some markers moved. On anything but a replica set the check refuses here, for the reason in the section
   on sharded clusters below. On a replica set it skips an item that can't have a matching event committed after the
   read.
   That's an item with tags that has a marker that didn't move, because such an event increments every tag marker of
   the item (ADR 147, I2). It's also an item without tags none of whose markers moved, because such an event increments
   one of them.
4. For every other item the check needs the query in the next section. When it can't run that query, it refuses.

Steps 1 to 3 need nothing but the markers, so they also work for a marker a 0.34 writer incremented. Step 3 removes
the second case of #1231 whenever the other append lacks one of the item's tags. It also keeps an untouched item out of the query, such as `type(X)` in `anyOf(type(X), tags(a, b))` when only
`a` moved.

### The check queries the events above the versions the read saw

For each item step 3 didn't skip, the store queries, inside the same transaction, for an event that matches the item
and has an `mv` element with a selection key of the item, the epoch the token saw and a version above it:

- For an item with tags, the selection key is the one a read after marker versions uses (ADR 148), the item's first
  tag key in canonical order. Every matching event has every tag of the item, so one key finds all of them.
- For an item without tags, every type key whose marker moved is a selection key, one branch each. A marker that
  didn't move holds no such event, and one that doesn't exist has no epoch to select on.

The query uses the `{mv.k, mv.e, mv.v}` index ADR 148 created, runs on the transaction's session, takes the first
match and doesn't apply the Spring stores' `queryOptions`. A match refuses the append, and no match passes it.

On a replica set, the store runs the query only when both of these hold, and refuses otherwise:

- The token saw the marker with an epoch, or didn't see it at all. A marker that existed without an epoch at the read
  was last written by 0.34, and its events may have no `mv`.
- The marker's u is the token's u. When u moved, a writer that writes no `mv` incremented the marker since the read,
  and its event can't be found by `mv`.

The query doesn't depend on `resumeFromMarkerVersions` (ADR 148). That setting is for deployments that can't run the
read-only transaction a snapshot read needs, and the check runs inside the append's own transaction. Every append
writes `mv`, `s` and the epoch whatever the setting says.

A key the token didn't see gets version 0 and the marker's current epoch. The marker didn't exist at the read, so
that epoch was created after it, and every `mv` element with that epoch is newer than the read.

`DcbCriteria.all()` has no selection key, so a `wholeStoreLock` condition keeps steps 1 and 2 and refuses whenever
the `all` marker moved.

### On a sharded cluster the check refuses when a marker moved

Two things stop working through a mongos. A transaction at read concern local or majority isn't guaranteed to read every
shard from one snapshot, so the query could read the events from before the markers the check just read. And a plain
read isn't one snapshot either, so a token can hold one marker from after a matching event E and another from before it,
while the read misses E. Step 3 would pass that token, because the marker from after E didn't move, and the sum check
would refuse it. A probe on two shards with `_dcb_checkpoints` range-sharded on `_id` showed this, with a fail point
holding E's commit on one shard. Natural timing didn't reproduce it in 1600 iterations.

So on anything but a replica set, steps 1 and 2 still apply, and any marker that moved refuses the append. That refuses
everything the sum check refused. It doesn't refuse everything 0.34 refused, because a token no longer holds the type
markers of an item with tags (ADR 147). An event of type T with another tag moved a marker of a 0.34 read of
`type(T).tags(a)`, and it moves no marker of this one.

The store asks the server once, when the store is created, with a `hello` command. A server too old to know `hello`,
such as MongoDB 4.2.8, answers with error code 59, and the store then uses `isMaster`. All three stores apply the same
test to the answer. The store counts as running on a replica set only when the answer has a `setName` and its `msg`
isn't `isdbgrid`. A mongos, a load balancer in front of one and a standalone server don't count. Any other failure of
the command makes creating the store fail, as the store's own initialization already does when it can't reach the
server. A wrong "no" costs a refusal the sum check would also make, and a wrong "yes" would let a matching append
through.

This doesn't make a plain read through a mongos safe. With the markers on one shard and the events on another, a token
can hold E's markers while the read misses E, and then no marker moves and the append passes. The sum check has the same
hole, so it isn't new. A read with `withVersions()` whose stream reports versions ran in a snapshot transaction, and in the
same probe it blocked during the window and the append was refused. A stream that reports none may have come f

adrs.title: A DCB type marker is split into stripes

adrs.text:
# 162. A DCB type marker is split into stripes

Date: 2026-10-30

## Status

Proposed. Decides the second part of [#1229](https://github.com/johanhaleby/occurrent/issues/1229). Amends
[ADR 21](0021-dcb-write-path-query-scoped-concurrency.md) on which markers an append increments when the setting below
is on, [ADR 147](0147-a-dcb-consistency-token-belongs-to-the-criteria-it-was-read-with.md) on the marker keys of an
item without tags, and [ADR 148](0148-dcb-snapshots-resume-from-marker-versions-not-positions.md) on what a marker key
looks like and on which keys saved versions need a marker for. Works with the append check of
[ADR 149](0149-the-mongodb-dcb-append-check-compares-each-marker-and-then-the-events-above-it.md).

## Context

Every DCB append increments one marker document per tag and one per type of its events (ADR 21). Two appends of the
same type always write the same `type:X` document, so MongoDB lets only one of them commit at a time, even when their
tags differ and no condition could ever see both. ADR 147 stopped tagged conditions from reading type markers, which
removed the false conflicts on the read side. The write side still serializes every append of a type.

A benchmark on the native store, 16 threads, conditional appends on a single-node replica set under heavy machine
load, gave an order of magnitude only. Appends of one type reached 46 to 119 per second, and appends of distinct types
320 to 822. The marker is the bottleneck for an application whose appends are mostly of one type.

The type marker is needed for one thing only. A condition with an item without tags, such as `type("TicketSold")`, has
to share a document with every append of that type, or a matching append could commit without the conditional one
noticing. ADR 147 said this part of #1229 depends on how positions are reserved. It doesn't. The argument below uses
shared marker documents only.

Released 0.34 nodes read and write `type:X` only, and nothing in a 0.34 node can be changed. Whatever 0.35 does has to
keep a 0.34 node that shares the store correct, or say plainly when it can't.

## Decision

### Stripes

The marker of a type is split into K stripes, with K = 8, a constant in the code.

- Stripe 0 keeps the key `type:X`, so every marker document and `mv` element that exists today stays valid.
- Stripe i, from 1 to K - 1, has the key `typestripe:i:X`. A key of its own prefix can't collide with a type's key,
  since `type:X#3` is the key of a legal type called `X#3`.
- The marker keys of an item without tags are every stripe of each of its types, whatever any setting says. So a read
  of such an item reads K documents per type, a conditional append on it compares and increments all K, and a read
  after versions selects on every stripe that has a marker (see "Saved versions with an absent stripe").
- By default an append increments stripe 0 of each type among its events, as 0.34 does.
- `spreadTypeMarkerWrites(true)` on the native, the Spring blocking and the Spring reactor `EventStoreConfig`, or
  `occurrent.event-store.mongodb.spread-type-marker-writes=true` in either Spring Boot starter, makes an append increment
  stripe `floorMod(appendId.value().hashCode(), K)` of each type instead. The store creates the `AppendId` once per
  append, before any retry, so every event of one append and every attempt use the same stripe.
- Tags are incremented as before.

The in-memory store derives the same keys and always writes stripe 0, so a saved `DcbMarkerVersions` means the same on
every store (ADR 148).

### Why a matching append can't get through

Take a condition with an item without tags on type X, and an append of an X event E committed after the read. E's
append increments stripe s of X, where s is 0 when its node has the setting off. The item's marker keys hold all K
stripes, so the conditional append compares stripe s with the token and increments stripe s too. If E committed before
the conditional transaction's snapshot, stripe s moved and ADR 149's check sees it. If E commits after, both
transactions write stripe s, and MongoDB lets only one commit. The stripe E picked never enters the argument, so any
function of the append would do, and so would a different setting on each node.

An item with tags doesn't read type keys at all (ADR 147), so stripes change nothing for it.

`all` and the tag markers stay as they are.

### Turning the setting on or off

Every 0.35 node reads all K stripes, whatever its own setting. So nodes on different settings can share a store, and a
rolling restart that turns the setting on or off is safe. This is the interleaving with node A on the default and node
B with the setting on:

1. A reads `type("TicketSold")`. Its token holds all eight stripes.
2. B appends a `TicketSold` whose `AppendId` picks stripe 3, so `typestripe:3:TicketSold` moves.
3. A appends with its token. Stripe 3 moved, so ADR 149's check queries it, finds the event and refuses. If B's append
   commits after A's transaction took its snapshot instead, both write stripe 3, and one of them aborts.

The other way round, a read on B and a matching append on A, is the same argument with stripe 0.

Turn the setting on only when no 0.34 node runs against the store. A 0.34 node's only key for an item without tags is
`type:X`, so an append on another stripe is invisible to it:

1. A 0.34 node reads `type("TicketSold")` and gets a token with the version of `type:TicketSold`.
2. A 0.35 node with the setting on appends a `TicketSold` whose `AppendId` picks stripe 3. It increments
   `typestripe:3:TicketSold` and doesn't write `type:TicketSold`. Seven appends in eight pick a stripe other than 0.
3. The 0.34 node appends with its token. `type:TicketSold` hasn't moved, so its check passes although a matching event
   was committed after its read. Its transaction shares no document with the 0.35 append, so nothing aborts it.

The same holds for any condition with an item without tags, such as `anyOf(tags(a), type("TicketSold"))`, for a
condition with no token, such as a 0.34 `failIfEventsMatch(type("TicketSold"))`, and for a condition an application
service builds from a read. Conditions whose items all have tags are safe, since both versions increment every tag of
an event.

With the setting off, 0.34 and 0.35 nodes can share a store in both directions. A 0.35 append writes `type:X`, which a
0.34 read sees. A 0.34 append increments `type:X`, which is stripe 0, and a 0.35 condition reads and increments every
stripe. So an upgrade from 0.34 is a rolling one again, as ADR 148 promises.

To go back to 0.34 after turning the setting on, turn it off and restart every process that appends to
the store, then downgrade. That includes a separate service, a migration or a tool with its own `EventStoreConfig`.
After the restart no process writes a stripe other than 0, so a 0.34 node sees every later append of a type. An event appended on another
stripe before that was committed before any 0.34 read that follows, so the read returns it. The stripe documents stay
behind, unused by 0.34.

### What it costs

| Operation | 0.34, one marker | 0.35, setting off | 0.35, setting on |
|---|---|---|---|
| An append | one type document written per type | the same, stripe 0 | the same, on its stripe |
| Two appends of one type with different tags | always conflict | always conflict | conflict when they pick the same stripe, about 1 in 8 |
| A read of an item without tags | one marker document per type | eight, in the same single query | eight |
| A conditional append on an item without tags | compares and increments one document per type | eight, so it writes eight documents, and still conflicts with every append of the type | the same as off |
| A read after versions on an item without tags | one `mv` branch per type | eight | eight |
| A token or saved `DcbMarkerVersions` of an item without tags | one entry per type | eight | eight |

An application that never turns the setting on pays for stripes and gets nothing back. Every read of an item without
tags reads eight marker documents per type instead of one, and every conditional append on one writes eight. The
writes can't be skipped when the local setting is off. Another node may have it on and append on stripe s during that
conditional's transaction, and only a document both transactions write makes MongoDB abort one of them. Nothing has
measured either cost.

A simulation of the benchmark above used tagged conditional appends, as with the setting on. With K = 8 it reached 202
to 446 appends of one type per second, and with K = 32 it reached 313 to 586, under the same machine load. K = 8 wins
back about half of what one marker loses against distinct types. In the three paired runs, K = 32 gave 1.49, 0.81 and
1.55 times K = 8, which is at most about half as much again, for four times the cost on every read and conditional
append of an item without tags.

Nothing has measured a conditional append on an item without tags under load either. It holds K document writes in its
transaction and conflicts with every append of the type, so I expect more retries than today, and more stripes would
make that worse.

### Saved versions with an absent stripe

ADR 148 reports versions only when every marker key of the boundary has a marker with an epoch. With the setting off,
stripes 1 to 7 come into existence only through a conditional append on an item without tags. So a snapshot of
`type(D)` or of `anyOf(tags(a), type(D))`, in an application whose appends of `D` are unconditional or conditioned on
tagged items only, would never get versions. Each snapshot would read its boundary in full, including everything from
before 0.35, for as long as the setting stays off.

So a stripe key may be saved as absent. `DcbMarkerVersions.MarkerVersion` gets an absent value, with no epoch, version 0
and an unstamped count of 0. A read that asks for versions reports a stripe it finds no marker for as absent. A tag key
still needs a marker, and a marker that exists without an epoch still gives no versions.

A read after saved versions treats an absent stripe like this:

- Still absent, it selects nothing on that stripe.
- Present now, the marker needs an epoch and an unstamped count of 0, or the read is refused with `DcbSnapshotInvalid`.
  The read then selects every `mv` element on that stripe with the marker's epoch, which is every version above 0.

This is sound for the same reason ADR 149's check can trust a marker that was absent at the read. Versions come from
one point-in-time read of the markers and the events (ADR 148). An append creates the marker of every key its events
have, in its own transaction, and the pruning rule of ADR 149 deletes a stripe only in a transaction that finds no event
of its type. So no event committed before the save has an `mv` element on a stripe that was absent at the save, and
every event that has one now was committed after it. Selecting all of them returns exactly that stripe's part of the
events after the save.

The unstamped count and the epoch cover the rest. Every event a 0.35 node writes has an `mv` element for each of its
own marker keys. A conditional append also increments the keys of its condition, but that adds no event, so with an
unstamped count of 0 every event of the stripe has an element. A 0.34 append of `X` touches only stripe 0. If it creates
`type:X` after the save, the marker has no epoch and the read is refused. A later 0.35 increment gives that marker an
epoch, but its unstamped count is then 1, so the read is still refused. If a 0.34 append increments a `type:X` that a
0.35 append created, it moves the unstamped count too, and ADR 148 refuses a moved one today. That's why stripe 0 can be
absent too. A stripe created after the save, pruned and created again has a new
epoch, and its prune removed every event of the earlier one, so the current epoch selects them all.

This removes the wait for versions on such a boundary. A type nobody has a

adrs.text:
# 30. Keep MatchAll as a DCB append condition, with its whole-store-lock limit documented

Date: 2026-06-28

## Status

Accepted. Amended by [ADR 147](0147-a-dcb-consistency-token-belongs-to-the-criteria-it-was-read-with.md). For a criteria item with at least one tag, the query reads and increments only its `tag:` markers.

## Context

ADR 0021 serializes DCB appends through per-attribute markers. An append increments a marker for each tag and each type of its events and of its condition's query, two appends that can match a common event share at least one marker and so conflict, and a read captures the sum of its query's marker versions as the consistency token, which the conditional append rechecks inside its transaction.

A `MatchAll` query (`DcbQuery.all()`) matches every event, and its only marker is `all`. So a `MatchAll` append condition conflicts with another `MatchAll` append (both touch `all`), but not with a tag-scoped or type-scoped append, which touches only its own tag and type markers and never `all`. A `MatchAll` condition is therefore not skew-safe against a concurrent scoped append: a scoped append can commit a matching event that the `MatchAll` condition never sees.

Making `MatchAll` fully skew-safe would require every append to also touch the `all` marker, which serializes every append in the store on one document. That is the global serialization ADR 0021 set out to avoid, so it is not an option. The open question is whether to keep `MatchAll` as an append condition at all.

## Decision

Keep it, and state the limit loudly rather than removing it.

A `MatchAll` append condition stays correct and useful wherever there is no concurrent scoped append:

- single-writer operations such as a migration, an admin fix-up, or a rebuild guard, where there is no concurrency to skew, and
- an empty-store or bootstrap guard, which is safe even against a concurrent second bootstrapper, because both carry a `MatchAll` condition and so conflict on the `all` marker.

The limit only bites when a `MatchAll` boundary is mixed with concurrent scoped appends on a multi-writer store. Rejecting `MatchAll` in an append condition would forbid the correct uses above to prevent that one misuse, and a correct-and-cheap whole-store lock is impossible as shown above. The proportionate choice is to keep the capability and name the unsafe pattern explicitly at the API: the Javadoc of `DcbQuery.all()` and `DcbAppendCondition.failIfEventsMatch`, and the user documentation.

## Consequences

- `MatchAll` append conditions remain available for single-writer and bootstrap use, where they are correct.
- A user who mixes a `MatchAll` boundary with concurrent scoped appends can still under-protect. This is now stated at the API, not only in this ADR and ADR 0021. It is not enforced in code.
- If the footgun is hit in practice, a later change can reject `MatchAll` in an append condition, making the unsafe pattern unrepresentable, at the cost of the single-writer and bootstrap uses.
